articles.title: Lula vira em Osasco, Cotia e mais cinco cidades e vence em 21 dos 39 municípios da Grande SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente reeleito reverteu vantagem em cidades como Osasco e Cotia. Diadema e Francisco Morato registraram os maiores percentuais de Lula (PT), enquanto Guararema e Santa Isabel tiveram as maiores votações proporcionais de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).
articles.summary: Presidente reeleito reverteu vantagem em cidades como Osasco e Cotia. Diadema e Francisco Morato registraram os maiores percentuais de Lula (PT), enquanto Guararema e Santa Isabel tiveram as maiores votações proporcionais de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).
articles.body:
O deputado federal André Janones abraça o presidente Lula, reeleito neste domingo — Foto: Rafael Peixoto/g1

O mapa de votação da Grande São Paulo mudou de cor após o resultado da eleição presidencial neste domingo (25). Lula (PT) terminou à frente na disputa em 21 dos 39 municípios da Região Metropolitana, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) foi o mais votado nas outras 18 cidades.

No primeiro turno, o cenário foi diferente: Flávio venceu em 25 municípios, contra 14 de Lula. No segundo turno, o petista reverteu o resultado em sete cidades, e não houve município em que o petista tenha vencido o primeiro turno e perdido a disputa no segundo ( veja lista abaixo ).

Lula superou 60% dos votos em Diadema e Francisco Morato, enquanto Flávio ultrapassou 60% em Guararema e Santa Isabel. Já em Ribeirão Pires, a diferença entre os dois candidatos ficou em apenas 102 votos.

Os municípios da Grande São Paulo que registraram virada de Lula foram: Osasco, Cotia, Jandira, Poá, Embu-Guaçu, Ribeirão Pires e Pirapora do Bom Jesus.

Desempenho de Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) na Grande SP — Foto: g1

Osasco: Flávio venceu o primeiro turno com 191.726 votos (45,46%), contra 182.778 (43,34%) de Lula. No segundo turno, o petista virou e venceu com 234.320 votos (52,36%), enquanto Flávio recebeu 213.187 (47,64%). A diferença foi de 21.133 votos a favor de Lula.

Cotia: Flávio havia obtido 65.331 votos (46,21%) no primeiro turno, contra 59.084 (41,79%) de Lula. No segundo, o petista chegou a 76.363 votos (51,20%), enquanto o adversário teve 72.794 (48,80%).

Jandira: Flávio liderou a primeira etapa com 25.516 votos (45,39%), contra 24.546 (43,66%) de Lula. No segundo turno, o petista venceu com 31.446 votos (52,50%), ante 28.452 (47,50%) do candidato do PL.

Poá: Flávio recebeu 31.643 votos (46,21%) no primeiro turno, enquanto Lula teve 29.359 (42,88%). Na segunda etapa, o petista virou o resultado e venceu com 37.133 votos (51,72%), contra 34.665 (48,28%) do adversário.

Embu-Guaçu: Flávio havia vencido a primeira etapa com 17.338 votos (46,50%), contra 15.697 (42,10%) de Lula. No segundo turno, o petista obteve 20.568 votos (51,52%), enquanto Flávio recebeu 19.357 (48,48%).

Ribeirão Pires: Flávio venceu o primeiro turno com 30.399 votos (47,21%), contra 26.550 (41,23%) de Lula. No segundo turno, a disputa terminou praticamente empatada: o petista venceu com 34.096 votos (50,07%), apenas 102 a mais que os 33.994 votos (49,93%) de Flávio.

Pirapora do Bom Jesus: a primeira etapa terminou com a menor diferença entre os candidatos entre as sete cidades. Flávio venceu por apenas oito votos, com 4.634 (45,69%), contra 4.626 (45,61%) de Lula. No segundo turno, o petista virou e alcançou 5.826 votos (54,38%), enquanto o adversário teve 4.888 (45,62%).

Os maiores redutos eleitorais de cada candidato

O ranking de votos absolutos entre os dois candidatos foi:

Guarulhos : Flávio Bolsonaro, com 380.962 votos.

São Bernardo do Campo : Lula, com 268.963 votos.

Santo André : Flávio Bolsonaro, com 219.136 votos.

Mogi das Cruzes : Flávio Bolsonaro, com 136.895 votos.

Barueri : Flávio Bolsonaro, com 116.985 votos.

Itaquaquecetuba : Lula, com 105.827 votos.

Os resultados do segundo turno também mostram municípios em que Lula e Flávio alcançaram seus maiores percentuais de votação na Grande SP.

Rio Grande da Serra: 58,01% (15.250 votos)

Na capital paulista, Lula também terminou à frente, com 3.864.354 votos, equivalentes a 55,50% dos votos válidos considerados no levantamento.

Flávio Bolsonaro teve seus maiores percentuais em:

São Caetano do Sul: 58,33% (70.741 votos)

Disputas apertadas em grandes municípios

Alguns dos resultados mais equilibrados ocorreram em municípios com eleitorados expressivos:

Em Santo André , Flávio terminou o segundo turno com 219.136 votos (50,29%), contra 216.589 (49,71%) de Lula, diferença foi de 2.547 votos;

Em Barueri , o candidato do PL recebeu 116.985 votos (50,70%), enquanto Lula teve 113.777 (49,30%), uma vantagem de 3.208 votos para Flávio;

Em Guarulhos , o candidato do PL recebeu 91.006 votos (50,92%), enquanto Lula teve 87.723 (49,08%);

Já em Suzano , o candidato do PL recebeu 91.006 votos (50,92%), enquanto Lula teve 87.723 (49,08%)

Em São Caetano do Sul , Flávio alcançou 58,33% dos votos, com 70.741, enquanto Lula recebeu 50.544 (41,67%);

Em Mogi das Cruzes , a diferença também foi mais ampla: Flávio teve 136.895 votos (54,27%), contra 115.339 (45,73%) de Lula

O petista manteve a liderança no segundo turno em cidades como São Paulo, São Bernardo do Campo, Carapicuíba, Mauá, Itapevi, Itaquaquecetuba, Ferraz de Vasconcelos, Franco da Rocha e Itapecerica da Serra.

Em São Bernardo do Campo, reduto eleitoral de Lula, o petista passou de 215.232 votos (46,77%) no primeiro turno para 268.963 (55,37%) no segundo. Em Carapicuíba, avançou de 94.231 votos (46,30%) para 121.023 (55,41%).

Em Mauá, o petista saiu de 102.086 votos (45,84%) para 130.276 (54,69%). Já em Itapevi, passou de 56.175 votos (47,23%) para 71.036 (56,64%).

Flávio, por sua vez, manteve a liderança em municípios como Guarulhos, Santo André, Mogi das Cruzes, Barueri, Suzano, Santana de Parnaíba, Cajamar, Caieiras, Arujá e Vargem Grande Paulista.

articles.title: IFCE oferta mais de 500 vagas em cursos técnicos gratuitos no Ceará | G1
articles.standfirst: O período para inscrições começa às 15h desta segunda-feira (26) e vai até às 23h59min do dia 15 de novembro de 2026. As aulas começam no próximo ano.
articles.summary: O período para inscrições começa às 15h desta segunda-feira (26) e vai até às 23h59min do dia 15 de novembro de 2026. As aulas começam no próximo ano.
articles.body:
IFCE abre seleção com 505 vagas para cursos técnicos. — Foto: Divulgação

O Instituto Federal do Ceará (IFCE) lançou, na última sexta-feira (23), um edital para seleção em cursos técnicos com 505 vagas nas cidades de Acopiara , Baturité , Fortaleza , Guaramiranga , Paracuru e Tabuleiro do Norte. As oportunidades são nas áreas de biotecnologia, gastronomia, informática e mais (confira abaixo a lista completa).

O período para inscrições começa às 15h desta segunda-feira (26) e vai até às 23h59min do dia 15 de novembro de 2026. As inscrições gratuitas podem ser feitas no sistema Q-Seleção .

As vagas são para cursos técnicos integrados (ensino médio + educação profissional) e técnicos subsequentes (educação profissional para egressos do ensino médio). As oportunidades são para os seguintes cursos:

Informática para Internet (Baturité e Tabuleiro do Norte)

Manutenção Automotiva (Tabuleiro do Norte)

Tradução e Interpretação de Libras (Fortaleza e Acopiara)

De acordo com informações do IFCE, a seleção será feita através da análise do histórico escolar do candidato, portanto não haverá prova . De acordo com o cronograma, a divulgação do resultado final está prevista para o dia 27 de novembro.

Na mesma data serão divulgados o cronograma e os procedimentos de heteroidentificação e de pré-matrícula. As aulas vão começar no primeiro semestre de 2027.

articles.title: Vídeo raro mostra tucano 'vomitando' ovos para alimentar filhotes | G1
articles.standfirst: Câmera instalada em uma propriedade rural no Mato Grosso do Sul registrou o momento em que a ave retira vários ovos da garganta e os oferece aos filhotes.
articles.summary: Câmera instalada em uma propriedade rural no Mato Grosso do Sul registrou o momento em que a ave retira vários ovos da garganta e os oferece aos filhotes.
articles.body:
Um comportamento curioso de um tucanuçu ( Ramphastos toco ), também conhecido como tucano-toco, foi registrado por uma câmera de monitoramento instalada em uma propriedade rural no interior de Mato Grosso do Sul. Nas imagens, a ave aparece alimentando seus filhotes com ovos que transportava dentro da garganta . Um a um, os ovos chegam ao bico do animal e são oferecidos aos filhotes no ninho.

O flagrante chama a atenção não apenas pela quantidade de ovos transportados, mas também pela habilidade do tucano em armazenar e recuperar os alimentos sem quebrá-los.

Segundo o biólogo Fernando Magnani, que dirigiu o Parque Ecológico de São Carlos (SP) por 34 anos, o registro é especialmente interessante porque documenta uma situação pouco observada em detalhes.

"A imagem que foi capturada pela pessoa que conseguiu registrar o tucano alimentando seus filhotes com uma série de ovos é uma imagem fantástica. Ela representa o que a gente já sabe ou vê muitas vezes de relance, mas a pessoa conseguiu capturar na íntegra", afirma.

Para o especialista, o vídeo também ajuda a compreender a participação dessas aves na cadeia alimentar.

"É realmente uma imagem rara e importante [...] não só para poder ilustrar um pouco sobre o animal, mas também mostrando às pessoas a sua importante característica ecológica", explica.

Vídeo raro mostra tucano 'vomitando' ovos para alimentar filhotes — Foto: Elaine de Almeida Aragoni

O registro foi feito por Elaine de Almeida Aragoni, criadora de conteúdo digital e produtora rural que vive no interior de Mato Grosso do Sul.

Ela instalou a câmera em uma mangueira, a poucos metros de sua residência, justamente para acompanhar o desenvolvimento dos filhotes de tucano.

"A câmera foi instalada para acompanhar o ninho dos tucanos. Inclusive, a poucos metros havia ninho de papagaios, e também tinha câmera registrando", conta.

Elaine não soube precisar se o flagrante específico aconteceu em outubro ou novembro, mas acompanhou a movimentação das aves durante aproximadamente dois meses.

Nesse período, registrou diferentes momentos da alimentação e do crescimento dos filhotes, até a saída deles do ninho.

"Acompanhei por cerca de dois meses, até os filhotes deixarem o ninho. Inclusive, tenho registros disso também", relata.

A produtora rural também observou os pais oferecendo diferentes tipos de alimento aos filhotes, incluindo filhotes de outras espécies de aves.

Apesar de acompanhar a rotina dos tucanos, ela não imaginava que eles fossem capazes de transportar vários ovos dessa maneira.

"Fiquei impressionada, não fazia ideia que isso era possível", afirma.

Como o tucano consegue transportar os ovos?

Elegância e funcionalidade! O tucano-toco, com seu bico impressionante, é um símbolo da biodiversidade e da importância da preservação das florestas tropicais. — Foto: Divulgação

Embora as imagens possam dar a impressão de que o tucano está regurgitando os ovos, Fernando Magnani explica que o comportamento está relacionado a uma característica anatômica dessas aves .

O tucanuçu possui capacidade de dilatação do esôfago , o que permite armazenar temporariamente alimentos e transportá-los antes de oferecê-los aos filhotes.

"O tucano-toco, assim como outras aves também, tem uma característica de dilatação do esôfago. E ali ele consegue armazenar o alimento e não entrar em processo de digestão. Ele consegue transportar esse alimento por longas distâncias", explica.

Esse mecanismo permite que a ave carregue não apenas ovos, mas também frutos e pequenos animais capturados durante a busca por alimento.

"Frutinhas, pequenos passarinhos, filhotes de passarinho e ovos, no caso aí, por exemplo, eles são transportados por longas distâncias nessa dilatação do esôfago. E depois, através de um processo de contração, ele consegue trazer esse alimento até o bico", detalha Magnani.

O bico, que pode parecer desproporcional ao tamanho do corpo, também desempenha um papel fundamental nesse processo.

Apesar das dimensões, a estrutura é muito leve e permite movimentos precisos, inclusive para manipular objetos delicados.

"Ele tem uma destreza, uma agilidade com esse bico que é muito leve, é levíssimo esse bico, apesar de ter uma estrutura muito sólida. Ele consegue ter uma agilidade muito grande a ponto de mexer muito pequenos objetos [...] É uma pinça para ele", compara o biólogo.

Por que o tucano come ovos de outras aves?

Conhecido pela dieta frugívora, tucano-toco também é predador — Foto: boytoad99 / iNturalist

Conhecido principalmente pelo consumo de frutas, o tucanuçu também possui hábitos predatórios. Ovos, filhotes e até outras aves podem fazer parte de sua alimentação.

Segundo Magnani, essa característica ganha importância durante o período reprodutivo, quando os adultos precisam garantir nutrientes para o desenvolvimento dos filhotes.

"O tucano, apesar dessa característica de alimentação com frutas, que as pessoas mais conhecem, na verdade ele se torna boa parte do ano um grande predador. Ovos, filhotes de aves no ninho, até aves um pouco maiores, já adultas, entram no cardápio dele", explica.

A proteína de origem animal tem um papel importante no crescimento dos filhotes , especialmente durante o período em que permanecem no ninho.

"Esse desenvolvimento muscular, ósseo, ele em boa parte é fornecido através de alimentação com proteína de origem animal. Então, ele não conseguiria que seus filhotes se desenvolvessem de forma rápida e também de forma saudável se ele alimentasse só com frutas", afirma.

Isso não significa que os alimentos vegetais deixem de ser importantes. As frutas continuam integrando a dieta e fornecem outros nutrientes necessários ao desenvolvimento das aves.

"Mas a base alimentar do filhote enquanto no ninho ou ainda dependente dos pais acaba sendo proteína de origem animal", acrescenta.

Predador, mas também responsável pelo equilíbrio da natureza

Tucano sendo perseguido por outra ave — Foto: anudibranchmom / iNaturalist

O hábito de consumir ovos e filhotes de outras aves pode causar estranhamento, principalmente entre pessoas que associam os tucanos à alimentação à base de frutas.

Magnani ressalta, porém, que a predação faz parte das relações naturais entre as espécies e contribui para o equilíbrio dos ecossistemas.

"Ele é um integrante de uma cadeia alimentar que foi forjada ao longo de milhões de anos, com vários componentes nessa cadeia", explica.

Segundo o especialista, a presença de predadores ajuda a regular as populações de outras espécies e integra uma dinâmica natural de equilíbrio.

"Você imagine se não tivesse um predador que roubasse ovos, que se alimentasse de filhotes também, a explosão populacional das outras pequenas aves", exemplifica.

O biólogo destaca que não se deve interpretar esse comportamento como uma característica negativa do tucano.

A predação é apenas uma das funções ecológicas desempenhadas pela espécie.

Além de predador, o tucanuçu exerce outra função fundamental para a conservação ambiental: a dispersão de sementes .

Ao consumir frutos e se deslocar entre diferentes áreas de vegetação, a ave transporta sementes que podem contribuir para o surgimento de novas árvores.

Essa capacidade se torna especialmente importante em regiões onde as florestas foram fragmentadas pela ocupação humana.

"Hoje, o tucano, em várias partes, por exemplo, do estado de São Paulo, é o último grande dispersor de sementes", afirma Magnani.

Segundo o biólogo, o porte da ave e sua capacidade de percorrer grandes distâncias permitem que ela transite entre fragmentos florestais separados por áreas agrícolas.

"É uma ave de um porte médio que consegue se deslocar a grandes distâncias entre os fragmentos florestais, porque nós devastamos quase toda a mata contínua, deixando fragmentos. E esse tucano ainda consegue levar sementes de um fragmento ao outro, facilitando a variabilidade genética de várias espécies de árvores", explica.

Essa função ajuda a manter a conexão ecológica entre áreas de vegetação que, de outra forma, poderiam ficar isoladas.

"Ele não é só um predador de ovos e ninhos, que também é importante, mas também é um grande dispersor", reforça.

Para Magnani, compreender essas diferentes funções é essencial para reconhecer a importância da espécie.

O vídeo registrado por Elaine mostra justamente uma dessas faces menos conhecidas do tucanuçu: uma ave que, além de espalhar sementes e contribuir para a regeneração das florestas, também participa das relações de predação que sustentam o equilíbrio dos ambientes naturais.

articles.title: Salon owners in Brierley Hill urge Budget VAT cut as staffing pressures grow
articles.summary: Marcus Perkins, who owns a hair and beauty salon in Brierley Hill, says he is scared for the future.
articles.body:
After 22 years running a salon, Marcus Perkins says he is increasingly worried about the future of the hair and beauty industry.

Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to employ staff and invest in apprenticeships, he says, while more salons are turning to self-employed models to survive.

"Seeing salons close on the high street is very scary," he said. "I'm very scared myself. Luckily it hasn't happened yet but who knows what the future holds?"

Perkins is among more than 2,000 salon owners who have signed an open letter calling on the Chancellor John Healey to cut VAT on hair and beauty services from 20% to 10% in this week's Budget.

The letter is backed by the British Hair Consortium (BHC), which argues rising business costs are placing increasing pressure on traditional salon employers.

However, the industry has also seen growing numbers of stylists move into self-employed arrangements, with hairdressers often renting a chair within a salon rather than being directly employed.

With salon ownership perceived to be out of reach for many, self-employment offered independence, flexibility and higher earnings, industry research suggested .

A Treasury spokesperson said hair and beauty businesses played an important role in supporting jobs, apprenticeships and thriving high streets.

They added that the sector had benefited from reforms to business rates.

While traditional salons said they faced rising pressures, a recent report from the British Beauty Council found that hair and beauty salons and shops made up almost a third of all leisure sites across UK retail centres.

It added that those businesses now accounted for greater share of smaller high streets and were equivalent to pubs, bars and cafes combined.

There were 50,400 VAT or PAYE registered hair and beauty salons in the UK as of March 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics . That compared to 49,300 in March 2024.

Salon owners say they have also been affected by increases in wage, pension and National Insurance (NI) costs.

The government's changes to employers' NI contributions and increases to the minimum wage have been defended by ministers as part of wider efforts to improve pay, support public services and drive economic growth.

The BHC said a reduction in VAT would help businesses take on more staff, invest in training and keep more salons trading on the high street.

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to £800m

Perkins believed it would make a significant difference.

"We can grow the business and employ more people," he said.

The salon owner runs M&M Spa in Quarry Bank, near Brierley Hill, where he says he has trained more than a dozen young people over the past two decades.

Among them is 21-year-old stylist Trearna Hart, who said many of her peers had struggled to establish careers after leaving college.

She said she was fortunate to find an employer willing to invest in her development.

This year alone, Perkins said he had spent about £2,000 on courses and travel costs to support her training.

"It's upsetting really," he said. "We help people, we train, we nurture, we mentor. We help the next generation because if we don't help the next generation, what happens to our future?"

The BHC claimed apprenticeship numbers had fallen sharply and warned the trend could worsen if pressures on employer-run salons continued.

Financial pressures and concerns over inconsistent training standards had led salons to take on fewer apprentices, with 53% of salon owners reporting a reduction in the number they trained, according to a Future of Hairdressing report.

Perkins believes businesses that employ and train staff are increasingly competing against models centred on self-employed workers.

He argues that creates an "unlevel playing field" because traditional salons often shoulder the costs of training future hairdressers.

Hart said the number of salons disappearing from high streets was a concern.

"At the rate it's going we're not going to have many salons left open and there's no-one going to be able to do hair," she said.

The challenges facing the sector are also worrying some customers.

Research from the British Beauty Council highlighted the role hair and beauty businesses play in supporting local high streets, encouraging spending and providing opportunities for social connection.

Dorothy Senior has visited M&M for hair and beauty treatments for the past 20 years.

She said the salon was about much more than appearances.

"Every time I come in I go home feeling so much better," she said. "It isn't just having nails and hair done, it's the whole package."

articles.title: What to know about China’s plenum as Xi seeks stronger Communist Party discipline
articles.summary: China’s political leaders and elites began a four-day meeting Monday to discuss strengthening the ruling Communist Party’s discipline, as Chinese President Xi Jinping pushes for greater loyalty and reliability from officials while deepening his yearslong campaign against corruption.
articles.body: HONG KONG — China’s political leaders and elites began a four-day meeting Monday to discuss strengthening the ruling Communist Party’s discipline, as Chinese President Xi Jinping pushes for greater loyalty and reliability from officials while deepening his yearslong campaign against corruption. This week’s closed-door gathering, known as the fifth plenum of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, comes roughly a year before Xi is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party’s leader and personnel changes to key leadership bodies. Xi began the meeting by delivering a work report and speaking about a draft policy decision on advancing “full and rigorous party self-governance,” according to Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency. The policy aims to make cadres more disciplined and effective and less corrupt. While Xi has consolidated his grip on power, analysts say the plenum will offer him an opportunity to further align what Chinese officials do with what Beijing wants. “The plenum is a chance to ensure the new generations rising the ranks share Xi’s assessment of the opportunities and risks China faces,” said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London’s Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. Here’s what to know about one of Beijing’s most significant political meetings this year. Xi targets underperforming cadres and corruption Xi’s anti-graft drive has been a defining feature of his rule since he came to power in 2012. Purges of officials — including some viewed as his political rivals — have been carried out on a scale that led critics to argue the campaign was also used to consolidate his power. But his focus has expanded to cracking down on underperforming cadres as well. In recent years, the number of officials punished for “formalism” and “bureaucratism” — misconduct such as dereliction of duty, inaction and reckless acts that seriously hinder development — has surged. Xi’s policy proposals reflect his emphasis on the party’s “self-revolution,” a concept centered on the party reforming itself through efforts such as rooting out corruption and building ideological commitment, analysts say. Osman said the disciplinary crackdowns are now aimed more at institutional longevity. “It’s less about purging elite rivals and more about building a disciplined system that can sustain Xi’s political priorities across leadership cycles,” she said. Record-high disciplinary campaigns also do not necessarily mean a rebound in corruption, but rather that Xi has been steadily raising the bar for the party’s expectations of officials, she added. Mingda Qiu, senior analyst of Eurasia Group’s China practice, said Beijing has been building its agenda for months. “The message is clear: The anti-corruption campaign is not winding down. Officials are not only tested for loyalty, but also for compliance and action,” he said. Xi said in a January meeting that while decisions by the party’s top leadership were smoothly implemented in general, inspections and audits found problems such as failures to comply and improper execution, according to an October article in the Qiushi Journal, a publication of the central committee. Xi warned against “two-faced people” who might profess political loyalty while privately defying orders and doing as they please. “During leadership transitions, we must keep our eyes sharp, elevate good cadres who are truly loyal and reliable, consistent in word and deed, and willing to take responsibility, and never allow ‘two-faced people’ or those driven by self-interest to slip through,” Xi was quoted as saying. Xi’s purges of top army officials will be put on display The number of empty seats in the conference hall this week will help observers gauge how widespread Xi’s purges have been. Neil Thomas, senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, and his colleagues Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang noted that while Xi’s civilian purges are record-breaking, 42 out of 44 officials affiliated with the military elected as full central committee members in 2022 have also been purged or disappeared. The central committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 full and alternate members. Thomas and his colleagues estimated that turnout this week could be less than 80%, potentially setting a record low at any plenum since the end of former leader Mao Zedong’s rule in 1976. Attention will also be on new demands on the officials who remain. Thomas expects tighter scrutiny of public spending and major projects, more use of technology to uncover corruption, and tougher consequences for officials who fail to deliver on Xi’s priorities. New personnel appointments are possible, though Xi may wait until a once-in-five-years Communist Party Congress next year to anoint his picks, said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London. If he does fill any openings, it will be with loyalists, he added. Hints at a Xi successor are unlikely The underlying theme of the fifth plenum is that it will be another opportunity for Xi to position himself for an unprecedented fourth term in office. Xi, who removed presidential term limits in 2018, is viewed by some as the most powerful Chinese leader since Mao. He is widely expected to be confirmed as party leader for the next term in the fall of 2027. Ahead of that, Thomas said new ideological language reinforcing Xi’s authority might emerge at this week’s meeting. He said the plenum should prepare the ground for Xi’s fourth term and reinforce expectations of political and policy continuity. “After Xi has purged so many of the people that he promoted at the last congress, watch for tougher scrutiny of the officials competing to join his next leadership team,” he said.

articles.title: UK weather: Storm Boelo clears but more wind and rain forecast
articles.summary: Another area of low pressure will pass close to the north-west UK with a Met Office yellow wind warning issued for Tuesday.
articles.body:
After a weekend of heavy downpours and severe gales, Storm Boelo is moving away from the UK and the weather is turning calmer.

However, this may not last long as another deep area of low pressure is already approaching from the Atlantic.

As this moves into north-west areas of the UK during Monday and Tuesday it will bring another dose of rain and gales.

Met Office yellow wind warnings have been issued for much of Scotland, northern areas of Northern Ireland, Wales and western England.

However, this latest weather system is unlikely to be as widely disruptive as Storm Boelo - or Storm Austen which came before it - and has not, so far, been named.

The next name on the list for the 2026/2027 season is Chloe.

Rain to parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland on Monday morning will move rapidly north-eastwards, reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland by around lunchtime.

It will also be rather misty and murky over some coasts and hills.

As the rain clears, slightly drier conditions will spread across the UK from the south-west.

While many areas will remain cloudy a few bright or sunny spells are possible, especially in Wales and south-west England.

Southerly winds will bring warmer air than of late, especially in the south where temperatures may peak at 18 or 19C.

After a breezy start to Monday, winds will strengthen once again during the day, with widespread gusts of 30-40mph and 50mph gusts likely in many coastal areas and 65mph in some locations.

It will turn even windier overnight and Tuesday as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland, the very strongest gusts could reach 70-85mph in the Hebrides.

Yellow wind warnings are in place covering both of these areas starting from Monday evening into late Tuesday evening.

Check here for the latest information on weather warnings and keep up to date with the forecast for your area via the BBC Weather website and app

The Met Office warning suggests that there is a low risk of significant impacts, with the chance of travel disruption, power cuts, damage to buildings and some flying debris. Some trees are likely to get blown over.

Storm Boelo contained a spell of damaging westerly winds which effectively funnelled through the highly populated Central Lowlands, increasing the likelihood of impacts. In contrast the winds in this system will be southwesterly, with areas of high ground providing a greater degree of protection for the biggest towns and cities.

There is a risk of some localised flooding with more heavy rain forecast. Some coastal flooding is also possible where large waves coincide with high tides.

High pressure will build close to the UK from midweek onwards meaning the weather should gradually calm down.

Showers will continue on Wednesday but most places are expected to be dry by the end of the day.

Under light winds on Thursday morning, mist and fog could cause some travel disruption across some parts of the country. This should largely clear to leave a dry day with sunny spells.

A weather front could bring rain back into western parts on Friday but high pressure is then expected to rebuild with most computer weather models suggesting a drier and calmer spell is likely to develop over the weekend and into next week.

articles.title: California wants to spend $25 billion to put homebuyers deeper in debt
articles.summary: Proposition 37 would let California issue $25 billion in bonds for down payment assistance, but more borrowing won't solve the housing shortage.
articles.body: California has a housing affordability problem. Homes are expensive. Down payments are enormous. Young families are struggling to buy their first house. So, what's California's latest idea? Get into the mortgage business with $25 billion in borrowing authority. Apparently, when housing becomes too expensive, the answer is to help people borrow even more money. BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT Welcome to Proposition 37. The $25 billion mortgage experiment On November's ballot, California voters will consider a proposal allowing the California Housing Finance Agency to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance down-payment assistance. Here's how it works. Buyers put down as little as 3%. The state-backed program provides a second mortgage covering up to another 17%. The buyer finances the remaining 80% through a traditional mortgage. WE MUST HELP MORE PEOPLE BUY A HOME. IT’S KEY TO THE AMERICAN DREAM Sounds terrific. Except there's one little detail. The 17% isn't free money. It's another loan. And by the way, isn’t this the kind of strategy that sparked the last Great Recession of 2008? By offering people more and more money they couldn’t afford? And this distinction matters enormously. Let's do the math THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COMES WITH A ZIP CODE: HERE'S WHERE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL WITHIN REACH Imagine buying an $800,000 California home. With a traditional 20% down payment, you'd need $160,000 upfront and borrow $640,000. Under Proposition 37, you could potentially put down just $24,000. The state-administered program would lend you another $136,000. Your first mortgage would still be $640,000. You've reduced your upfront cash requirement by $136,000. But you've also increased your total mortgage debt by $136,000. Assume a hypothetical 6.5% interest rate on the first mortgage and 7% on the second, both over 30 years. Get into the mortgage business with $25 billion in borrowing authority. Apparently, when housing becomes too expensive, the answer is to help people borrow even more money. Your monthly principal and interest payments would increase from approximately $4,045 to $4,950. That's roughly $900 more every month. Property taxes, insurance and maintenance aren't included. Congratulations. You got into the house with less cash. AMERICA'S HOUSING MARKET COULD RUN OUT OF SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOMES Now you have a bigger monthly bill. Actual program interest rates haven't been established, so those numbers are illustrative. The government isn't giving away $25 billion To be fair, Proposition 37 isn't a $25 billion taxpayer-funded giveaway. The proposal uses revenue bonds intended to be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments, not California's general fund. The state's independent legislative analyst estimates no direct state or local government costs. Supporters argue that helping buyers finance newly constructed homes could encourage builders to increase supply. That's a legitimate economic argument. But it raises a bigger question. Does helping people borrow more money make houses cheaper? Not necessarily. It could actually make prices go up. We just saw this during COVID-19. You can't finance your way out of a housing shortage Imagine a neighborhood with 100 families trying to buy 80 homes. Now give more families access to larger financing packages. How many homes are available? Still 80. Unless builders increase supply, additional purchasing power can put upward pressure on prices. That's basic economics. California needs more homes, not simply more creative ways to finance expensive ones. Make it easier to build. Reduce unnecessary permitting delays. Address construction costs. Allow more housing where people actually want to live. Those measures attack the underlying shortage. Your first mortgage would still be $640,000. You've reduced your upfront cash requirement by $136,000. But you've also increased your total mortgage debt by $136,000. More borrowing primarily attacks the down payment. Those are not the same problem. The question California should answer There are families with excellent incomes who can afford monthly mortgage payments but struggle to accumulate six-figure down payments. A carefully structured loan program could help some of them become homeowners sooner. But helping buyers qualify for debt shouldn't be confused with reducing the price of housing. And the second mortgage still has to be repaid. California's proposal illustrates a question every homebuyer should ask before accepting financial assistance: Am I buying a more affordable home, or am I simply finding another way to afford the home? CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Because those are two very different financial outcomes. And no matter how creatively California packages the financing, one rule of personal finance never changes. articles.title: ‘We want justice, not a parade’: Caribbean seeks reparations for 'role in slave trade'
articles.summary: As King Charles III and Queen Camilla prepare for a nine-day tour of the Caribbean, calls are growing across the region for Britain to apologise for its
articles.body: As King Charles III and Queen Camilla prepare for a nine-day tour of the Caribbean, calls are growing across the region for Britain to apologise for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, pay reparations and loosen its remaining colonial ties.The royal visit, which begins in the Bahamas on Tuesday, comes amid renewed debate over the monarchy's place in the region and demands from activists and political leaders for Britain to address the legacy of slavery.The Bahamas National Reparations Committee has criticised the practice of organising schoolchildren to welcome the royals, saying they would be made to “stand in the sun and wave for the Crown that has taken everything from their ancestors and comes back smiling”.Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the committee and a psychology professor at the University of the Bahamas, said the visit should prompt people to question the country's continued relationship with the monarchy.“Why do we still have a king? What does this person really represent to us? Why is he coming and how will that benefit us?” she said, as quoted by Associated Press.Charles last visited the Bahamas in July 1973, when he was a prince and the archipelago was preparing to end nearly 300 years of British rule and become independent. The Bahamas remains a Commonwealth realm, however, with Charles as its head of state, alongside six other Caribbean nations.During his three-day stay, Charles is expected to visit Clifford Park, where the Bahamas' black, turquoise and yellow national flag was first raised more than 50 years ago.Reparations demands follow royals across the regionThe Bahamas is the first stop on the tour, which will also take Charles to Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda. The trip will bring the king into a region where governments and campaigners have increasingly challenged Britain's handling of its colonial past.Jamaica took its reparations case to Charles in early September, and the matter has since been referred to the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. The legal move was unprecedented, although the British government has repeatedly rejected calls for reparations or a formal apology for slavery.Jamaica, which has pushed in recent years to remove Charles as head of state and become a republic like Barbados did in 2021, is not on the royal itinerary. For some Jamaicans, the absence reflects a growing rejection of the monarchy. Rastafarian Steven Bennett, 51, said a royal visit would be inappropriate while the legacy of slavery remains unaddressed. “We don't need any royal wave or photo-taking while the wounds of our ancestors are still being ignored. He still refuses to formally apologise for chattel slavery,” Bennett said. “Until the British monarchy is ready to stand on Jamaican soil, look us in the eye, apologise, and talk about actual repair and restitution, he has no business here. We want justice, not a parade.”Jamaica has in recent years pushed to remove Charles as head of state and become a republic, following Barbados, which made the transition in 2021.Guyana, the next stop after the Bahamas, was the site of the 1823 Demerara rebellion, one of the largest slave uprisings in the region. Thousands of enslaved people rose up on plantations, including one owned by the father of former British prime minister William Gladstone. More than 200 enslaved people were killed in the aftermath, with some beheaded and their heads displayed on poles.In a recent interview with ITV News, Guyanese President Irfaan Ali said Charles had “rightfully recognised slavery as the darkest days in human history”.“Moving to the apology is the next step,” Ali said, adding that Britain had exploited the region, destroyed lives and contributed to underdevelopment.Charles is expected to meet Ali and elected leaders of Indigenous Amerindian villages, known as toshaos, during the Guyana leg of the visit. But not all community leaders have been included.Nikita Miller, toshao of Chinese Landing, a rural Indigenous community in northern Guyana, said she had not been invited. She wanted an opportunity to raise concerns about a longstanding dispute over community land with miners seeking to extract gold, an issue she said affects other Indigenous villages as well.“We have been suffering,” Miller said. “We want the government to respect Indigenous rights... We have long-standing issues with our land.”She said the royal visit might benefit Guyana as a whole but was unlikely to bring change to Amerindian communities.Jamaica's republican ambitions reflect changing attitudesAfter Guyana, Charles is scheduled to travel to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, where he will meet leaders from the organisation's 56 member states. Climate change, trade and development are expected to feature in discussions, though some Caribbean leaders want reparations for slavery to receive greater attention.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Maine homeowner bought land in front of his neighbour’s cottage and sued him for trespassing; court upheld the neighbour’s right to reach the beach
articles.summary: A property dispute at Popham Beach in Maine has ended with the state's highest court upholding a neighbour's right to access the beach in front of his
articles.body: A property dispute at Popham Beach in Maine has ended with the state's highest court upholding a neighbour's right to access the beach in front of his cottage. The case began after Richard Tappen purchased a parcel of land that lay in front of Clark Hill's property and subsequently sued him for trespassing. The two families had owned beachfront cottages in the area for decades, but disagreed over who had the right to use the disputed land. In January 2026, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court upheld a lower court's ruling in Hill's favour.Why did a Maine homeowner sue his neighbour over beach accessAccording to Maine Public's report, the dispute involved two neighbouring families at Popham Beach Estates, where beachfront cottages have been part of their lives for generations. Richard Tappen purchased a parcel of land that extended across the area in front of Clark Hill's cottage. He later took Hill to court in 2022, accusing him of trespassing on the property.The disagreement centred on whether Hill could continue using the beach despite Tappen's claim to the land. For Hill and his family, the area was more than a strip of privately disputed coastal property. It was a place they had long regarded as accessible for recreation.The case raised a question that often arises in coastal communities, where homes sit close to the shoreline and residents may have used the same stretches of beach for years. Owning the land and having a long-established way of reaching the water do not always lead to the same understanding of property rights.Maine Public reported that the Maine Supreme Judicial Court ultimately agreed with the lower court's decision that Hill had an implied easement for recreational use of Popham Beach. This meant the court recognised his right to use the disputed area for recreation despite Tappen's ownership claim.How did the disagreement over the beach developAn earlier account of the dispute published by Monday Morning Economist on September 18, 2023, provides further background on the families' disagreement. It reported that the Hill family had been visiting the area since the 1940s, long before the legal battle reached the courts.The conflict escalated in April 2021, when the Tappens sent the Hills a letter demanding they and their guests stop crossing the property and using the beach, the publication says. The notice stated that the land belonged to the Tappens and that the Hills should not use it any longer.The Hills, however, believed the beach was a shared area within their residential subdivision. Their position rested on the longstanding use of the space and their understanding that residents could reach the beach in front of their homes.Monday Morning Economist also reported that the Hills had built structures including a boardwalk, a deck, a ramp and a shed in the disputed area. The Tappens wanted these removed, arguing that they stood on land they had purchased.The disagreement concerned how the land had been used over time, what the families believed they were entitled to do and whether the purchase of the parcel gave the new owners the right to prevent that use.What did the court decide about the right to reach the beachThe Maine Supreme Judicial Court upheld the lower court's ruling in January 2026, confirming Hill's right to use Popham Beach for recreational purposes. Maine Public reported that the decision affirmed an implied easement, a legal right that allows someone to use another person's land for a particular purpose under recognised circumstances.The ruling in this case meant that Tappen’s claim of ownership did not automatically bar Hill from using the beach for recreational purposes. Rather than accepting the argument that Hill had trespassed on the property, the court upheld the right established by the lower court.The ruling did not mean that every stretch of privately owned coastal land in Maine was automatically open to everyone. Instead, it upheld the particular recreational access right recognised in Hill's case.Importance of the Popham Beach ruling beyond the two familiesThe dispute has broader implications for communities where residents have long relied on shared access to coastal areas. It is an example of the tension between private property ownership and the use of spaces that people have come to regard as common land.The Hills relied on the idea of a prescriptive easement, a legal claim based on long-term use of property. Their argument reflected their belief that the beach access they had enjoyed over the years should not disappear simply because another family acquired the land.The two families attempted to negotiate an arrangement before the dispute proceeded through the courts, according to Monday Morning Economist. However, those efforts failed to produce an agreement. The publication reported that the Tappens had been willing to permit access if the Hills paid $30,000 each summer.You use AI every day. articles.title: Storm Boelo: Electricity restored to all of Northern Ireland
articles.summary: The Met Office has issued two new yellow weather warnings for parts of Northern Ireland.
articles.body:
Electricity has been restored to all properties across Northern Ireland after Storm Boelo, Northern Ireland Electricity Networks (NIE) has said.

Shéa Clarke, who was stranded on Lusty Beg island in County Fermanagh, said that "safety comes first" and as "long as we don't run out of Guinness or chips".

At the weekend, the storm saw gusts of wind reach almost 80mph in some areas and led to flights and ferries being cancelled.

A Met Office yellow warning for strong winds, mainly along the Antrim and Down coasts, lasts from 18:00 GMT on Monday until 03:00 Tuesday.

Clarke was attending a wedding at the resort located in Lower Lough Erne.

"You could see the waves were rough and the wind was going.

"I've enjoyed myself the staff have been great and obviously it's too dangerous to cross and the boat can't cross so safety comes first," Clarke said.

"Some people have slept in cars, some people have slept on sofas there's been 8 people in one room sleeping on the floor.

"But the spirit has been good the craic is 90".

A second wind warning along the north coast of Antrim and Londonderry comes into place at 03:00 GMT on Tuesday until 21:00 GMT.

The Met Office is expecting gusts up to 50mph (80km/h) in Monday's warning zone, and up to 65mph (105km/h) on exposed coastal areas.

Gusts up to 60mph (105km/h) are again expected in Tuesday's warning, with stronger winds for more exposed coastal areas.

Olivia Millar, a cabin crew member based in London, was also a guest at the wedding and said the plan was to be in South Africa on Monday night.

"It hasn't felt like real life but everyone's been amazing and we've just made the most of it.

"We've drunk to pass the time and had a really good barbecue yesterday".

Staff at Lusty Beg Island Resort & Spa took care of guests who couldn't get off the island.

Michael Cadden, managing director at hotel, said they are "delighted at how staff and customers have dealt with this".

"The ferocity and the longevity of this storm was unlike anything we've experienced on the island before.

"This was a crisis, but we've now arranged to transport and are getting all our staff and customers safely home".

Kacper Dymarczyk, a bartender, was locked down with the guests and had to work through the storm.

"It was great craic, seeing other people drinking" he said as he laughed.

Dymarczyk added that there was "no concern" of running out of anything as they are "well stocked at all times".

Meanwhile in the Republic of Ireland, an ESB spokesperson said there are "a number of homes, farms and businesses still without electricity" on Monday morning, and that teams are working to restore the power to all properties.

About 5,000 homes, farms and businesses were still without electricity on Sunday evening in the Republic of Ireland.

Although some faults occurred overnight in Northern Ireland, and are showing on NIE's Powercheck tool , they are not believed to be storm related.

NIE said around 12,500 properties were without power at one stage after Storm Boelo.

Flights were cancelled at airports across the island of Ireland at the weekend including about 40 flights at Belfast International Airport and about 30 at Dublin Airport.

A spokesperson for Translink said that some bus services were diverted over the weekend due to fallen debris and rail restrictions were put in place in affected areas.

"Stormy conditions also increase 'leaf fall' at this time of year which can impact train services and our infrastructure crews will be deployed to clear any debris potentially blocking railway lines," they added.

On Sunday, the Department for Infrastructure (DfI) said around 470 incidents had been reported to the department, including fallen trees and flooding.

The Foyle Bridge was closed on Saturday due to high winds but reopened again on Sunday evening.

Foyle SDLP MLA Mark H Durkan said he understood the need to close the Foyle Bridge during Storm Boelo, but said its prolonged closure caused major traffic congestion throughout the city.

Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today , Durkan said redirecting vehicles to the lower deck of the Craigavon Bridge caused a traffic build-up and showed that the city was in desperate need of a third bridge.

"The infrastructural capacity of Derry needs increased; I don't think two vehicular bridges for a city of this side and a population of this city is enough."

In the Republic of Ireland, wind and rain warnings have also been issued for most counties along the south and west coasts on Monday evening.

Much improved weather conditions are expected on Wednesday with calmer and sunnier weather in the forecast.

articles.title: Delegations meet in Iran with Middle East on edge over potential for renewed fighting
articles.summary: High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting between Iran and Israel and the United States, Iran’s Foreign Ministry said.
articles.body: High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting between Iran and Israel and the United States, Iran’s Foreign Ministry said. The talks come as many in Iran are anxious about a possible return to all-out war. Israeli and American leaders have been sharpening their threats ahead of elections in both countries, while Iranian leaders have remained defiant. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, were to meet with Iran’s top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington. The war in Yemen and strikes by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also topics of the talks, according to two regional officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in the Iranian capital that the agenda for the meeting was not set, but the talks would “undoubtedly address the most pressing threats to regional security.” Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find “ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability.” Qatari mediators also traveled to Tehran on Sunday, working in coordination with the U.S., as part of efforts to de-escalate regional tensions, according to a regional official speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the talks. Pakistan and Qatar helped broker an agreement in June aimed at having Iran fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, ending a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and opening negotiations on a broader settlement addressing Iran’s nuclear program. The deal unraveled quickly, however, as both sides renewed attacks. With worries about renewed fighting ahead of Israel’s election on Tuesday and the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the U.S., Baghaei on the weekend said Tehran had not closed the window of diplomacy and that messages were being passed to the U.S. via intermediaries. With negotiations long stalled, he said that the U.S. appears to be persisting in unilateral demands and that President Donald Trump and U.S. officials repeatedly use the phrase “complete surrender,” which Baghaei said no Iranian accepts. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meantime, repeated his warning on Sunday that Iran or its proxies could attack ahead of the close elections to disrupt the vote, citing intelligence. “The (military) is ready both to defend and to strike,” he said in a video statement, adding: “You will suffer disproportionate blows far greater than you can imagine.” Israel’s Channel 12 reported Sunday night that Netanyahu and his military chief of staff clashed over an instruction by Netanyahu to carry out an “action” that the army believes could quickly trigger a resumption of the conflict with Iran. Netanyahu’s office later described the report as “fake news.” In a post on X, Defense Minister Israel Katz said that reports about “rifts between the political leadership and the IDF concerning Iran are completely baseless and false.” “I state unequivocally that there has been no intention by Israel of initiating an attack on Iran before the elections in Israel,” Katz said. “We made it clear that should Iran attack Israel, we would respond with great force.” In Tehran, when asked whether Iran was planning attacks, Baghaei on Monday only said that “the Israeli regime is highly skilled at carrying out false-flag operations.” “The Islamic Republic of Iran will not hesitate to exercise its inherent right to self-defense to protect Iran’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independence,” he said. Yemen has become a widening front in the Iran war that began in February, with the Houthis increasingly launching attacks on Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government battling the rebels. The conflict has intensified since forces from the internationally recognized government and Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that largely stopped the fighting in the country’s civil war. Early Monday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the rebel group had fired ballistic missiles at military gatherings and weapons depots belonging to Saudi-backed government forces in Aden and Lahj provinces. He claimed the attacks destroyed military equipment and caused casualties but did not provide evidence. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify the claims. Meantime, residents in Houthi-held Sanaa and on the Red Sea coast reported a series of explosions. Houthi media said airstrikes targeted a solar power system and a water well in Sanaa, but offered no proof. In the port city of Mokha, recently seized by the Houthis, residents said rockets hit several buildings including a hospital. Houthi-run al-Masirah channel also reported strikes in Saada, in northern Yemen, and in southwestern Taiz province, where the rebels and Saudi-backed government forces have been fighting for weeks. The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said an operation in Houthi-controlled territory destroyed five tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and another missile storage.

articles.title: Palestinians are opening their doors to the displaced of besieged Hebron
articles.summary: Israel’s assault on the West Bank city has forced thousands of people to flee their homes.
articles.body:
The Farsh Al-Hawa area in the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank is unrecognisable after Israeli forces demolished a three-story building and industrial facilities there. Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds the West Bank portfolio in the Ministry of Defence, said he ordered their destruction.

It all started on Friday, when two Palestinians attacked an Israeli military checkpoint in Farsh Al-Hawa, killing two soldiers and injuring others.

Since then, Hebron, the West Bank’s economic capital, has been attacked and put under lockdown by Israeli forces.

Israel has announced a sweeping military assault in the city , targeting the neighbourhood of the gunmen, who were killed on Friday. Israeli forces have already forcibly displaced more than 2,000 Palestinians. City officials say almost half of the displaced are babies and children under 18, along with 81 pregnant women and 204 elderly.

Fahd Ahmaro was forced to leave his home, along with his family. He told Al Jazeera that he planned to stay but felt compelled to seek shelter outside his neighbourhood because the women and children were terrified.

“We left with nothing but the clothes on our backs. Our savings, belongings and documents are all in the house,” he said. “I tried to go back after I got my family out safely, but I couldn’t. It’s not safe any more.”

Palestinian authorities in Hebron have declared a state of emergency and created a crisis group, bringing together government agencies, the private sector and civil society, to respond after thousands of people in the city were forced to flee their homes.

Riyadh Khamis, who serves on the committee, told Al Jazeera that philanthropists who could not bear the thought of fellow Palestinians staying in temporary shelters opened their homes to the displaced.

“Hebron is known for its social solidarity and generosity. Our city was the first to provide aid during the COVID lockdown and during the genocide,” Khamis told Al Jazeera. “Today, our neighbours needed help so we all rallied.”

Real estate developer Mohamed Al-Rujoob is one of the philanthropists who sprang to action at the start of the assault on the city.

Al-Rujoob, who owns several apartments in Dura, a town close to Hebron, announced that the properties would be made available for displaced families, prompting other owners to do the same. He now hosts three extended families in his apartments, including 30 children.

“We must preserve people’s dignity. Today, we host these good people. Tomorrow, who knows? It might be us who need shelter. We’re all under the same occupation and we’re all vulnerable,” he said.

The Israeli army says Hebron is on lockdown, which affects nearly 1 million Palestinians who live in the city and the rest of the district.

Restrictions on movement have had a severe impact on the West Bank’s largest district. Schools have moved to online classes, while Hebron’s universities have made similar arrangements for their 18,000 students until the Israeli operation ends.

The measures are essential for Palestinian students who are stuck in their homes and neighbourhoods, including the besieged Fawwar refugee camp in Hebron, home to nearly 8,000 Palestinians. Israeli soldiers closed the camp’s entrance gate on Saturday, barring residents from entering or leaving, even on foot.

Abdel Fattah Al-Ttitti, a school teacher who lives in the camp and works in a Hebron school, said “we are locked in”.

“If, God forbid, somebody needs medical attention, we may be able to get them to the clinic in Masafer Yatta, but that clinic is poorly equipped. If there’s a medical emergency, they can’t help,” Al-Ttitti told Al Jazeera.

He is glad that schools announced online classes. “Until this campaign is over, there’s no other way,” he said.

Many in Hebron believe that Israel’s military campaign in the city has a political dimension, with Israelis heading to the polls on Tuesday for a general election.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing coalition is vying for every right-wing vote. Violence against Palestinians has proved an expedient campaign tactic for politicians such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Minister of Settlement Affairs, Orit Strook.

Both right-wing ministers have homes in illegal settlements in the Hebron area and support the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from the occupied West Bank and Gaza, which they refer to as “encouraging voluntary migration”.

articles.title: John Healey's Budget to shield low-income pensioners from income tax
articles.summary: Changes are needed to prevent the full, flat-rate state pension becoming liable for income tax after it rises in April.
articles.body:
Pensioners on low incomes will be shielded from income tax by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget on Wednesday.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to increase by 3.9% to £13,036.40 a year from April. This would take the payment above the £12,570 personal tax allowance and therefore be liable for income tax if no changes are made.

The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension. Healey will explain this pledge will be met by plans for a new tax allowance for low-income pensioners.

Healey's plans come as the Conservatives and Reform UK unveil their alternative Budget proposals, including deep cuts to the welfare bill.

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

An insider's guide to Budget Day: 'Don't fall off the kerb'

How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?

The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.

More specific details, including how many pensioners this will affect, have yet to be confirmed by the Treasury.

The Budget is due to be printed this evening, with Healey's speech likely to be fine-tuned right up until it is delivered on Wednesday lunchtime.

Treasury sources concede it will not involve the scale of tax and spending announcements seen from Labour and Conservative governments in recent years.

The Tories are calling on the chancellor to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.

Reform is recommending the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper has called on the government to agree a new growth and defence partnership with the EU, including joining the single market. She argued this would help "ease the huge tax burden weighing people down".

The Green Party has urged Healey to use his first Budget to "make the UK affordable", including by funding energy bill support by ending a tax relief for data centres.

Senior Green politicians, including leader Zack Polanski, MPs and peers, made clear their suggestions in a letter to Healey.

articles.title: “No TV, no phones…”: How Asin and her husband are raising their daughter away from screens; “She can speak about 12 languages”
articles.summary: Actor Asin Thottumkal and her husband, Micromax co-founder Rahul Sharma, have taken a screen-free approach to raising their eight-year-old daughter, Arin
articles.body: Actor Asin Thottumkal and her husband, Micromax co-founder Rahul Sharma, have taken a screen-free approach to raising their eight-year-old daughter, Arin Rayn Sharma. According to Rahul, their home has no television, and Arin has not been given access to mobile phones or other screens. Instead, books occupy a central place in her childhood, with the family keeping reading material well beyond her current school level.In a 2025 interview with MyGov India, Rahul spoke about his marriage to Asin, her role in their family and the way she approaches their daughter's upbringing. He credited his wife with much of the work that goes into raising Arin and said their home environment reflects her contribution.No television or mobile phones at homeRahul said the couple have not introduced screens into Arin's life so far. “We have not given Arin any screens thus far. Therefore, no TVs or mobile phones. We only have books at home. We probably have more books at home than Arin has at her school,” he said. Arin is currently in Class 2, but her parents have already collected books intended for much older students.“She is in Class 2 right now, but we already have books for Classes 8 and 9 at home. I quip once in a while, saying, ‘Let her appear for the Class 10 board exam as well. What difference does it make?’ It’s all Asin’s contribution to us,” Rahul added. Rahul gave Asin the credit for putting this approach into practice and for the role she has played in shaping their daughter.Arin can speak about 12 languagesRahul also spoke about Arin's interest in languages. He said their daughter can understand and speak about 12 languages, including Korean, Japanese, Thai and Chinese. “I am finding it difficult to speak even two languages. We are stuck with English and Hindi,” he said. His remark offered a glimpse into Arin's interests, although he did not explain how she learned the languages or how proficient she is in each one.For parents, the family's approach raises an interesting question: how much of a child's everyday environment is shaped by the habits and choices adults make at home? In Arin's case, Rahul's account places books and language learning at the centre of family life.Rahul on Asin's role in the familyRahul's praise for Asin extended beyond parenting. He described her as a source of support who understands his ambitions and encourages him through difficult periods. “Marrying Asin was the most important thing that worked well for me. She is the rock behind me. If anything happens, whatever it is, she is the one who says, ‘Don’t worry… you just move forward.’ She understands me and my passion. She is a blind believer. If you have such people around you, life becomes very easy,” he said in the interview.He also spoke about the importance of having a supportive partner. “Our partner should be the person who lifts us, not one who pulls us from behind,” he said, adding that the same principle applies to friendships. “She is that person for me… she lifts me. Her contribution to my life is more than what I can explain,” he added.Rahul said that while he faces challenges outside the home, Asin takes care of the challenges within their family. “You are not just fighting a war outside, but you also have to face a similar one within your home, right? She (Asin) is the one who takes care of the latter [in our home]. I have never seen a person like her in my life,” he said.From a successful film career to family lifeAsin began her career with commercials before making her Malayalam film debut in Narendran Makan Jayakanthan Vaka in 2001. She gained wider recognition with the Telugu film Amma Nanna O Tamila Ammayi (2003), opposite Ravi Teja. She made her Hindi film debut opposite Aamir Khan in Ghajini (2008. The film became a major box-office success and was the first Hindi film to cross the ₹100-crore net collection mark in India.Asin went on to star in films including London Dreams (2009), Ready (2011), Housefull 2 (2012), Khiladi 786 (2012) and Bol Bachchan (2012). Her last film was All Is Well (2015), opposite Abhishek Bachchan. She married Rahul Sharma in 2016 and subsequently stepped away from acting.Don’t just take screens away; give children something to turn toWhen parents reduce screen time, the bigger question is what fills the space left behind. Books, puzzles, drawing materials and activities children can explore independently give them alternatives to reach for when they are bored. Instead of making every request for a phone a confrontation, parents can build predictable routines around these activities and join in without turning them into lessons. The aim is not simply to keep screens out of a child's hands, but to make other ways of spending time familiar and enjoyable.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2018, a six-bedroom Manhattan penthouse was listed for $27.5 million; seven years later, Scarlett Johansson and Colin Jost bought the 6,000-sq-ft home for $13 million, less than half its original asking price
articles.summary: Every New Yorker you meet will tell you how much they dream of owning a home in the city.
articles.body: Every New Yorker you meet will tell you how much they dream of owning a home in the city. Ask a real estate agent, though, and they’ll tell you that some Manhattan properties sit on the market for months, even years, before finding a buyer. This Upper East Side co-op took nearly seven years, and a series of price cuts, before Scarlett Johansson and Colin Jost finally snapped it up.First listed for $27.5 millionThis Manhattan penthouse was first listed in 2018. The asking price was $27.5 million, according to Architectural Digest. Craig and Deborah Cogut were the sellers, The Real Deal reported. They bought the apartment for $13 million in 2006. With no luck finding buyers, the asking price was lowered over the years. By the end of 2024, the price had fallen to less than half the original figure. In fact, the sale price matched exactly what the couple had paid almost two decades earlier. Whatever profit they had hoped for never materialised.Actor Scarlett Johansson and comedian Colin Jost, who married in 2020, were looking for a place in the city when they came across this listing. By early 2025, the celebrity couple had purchased the penthouse for $13 million, according to The Wall Street Journal.Inside the penthouseSpanning 6,000 square feet across three floors, the Upper East Side co-op features six bedrooms, seven bathrooms and sweeping views of Central Park. The penthouse is in a pre-war building designed by architect Rosario Candela in the 1930s. It has five terraces, eight balconies and six wood-burning fireplaces. The unit occupies the building’s upper floors.A private lift opens into a central gallery, where floor-to-ceiling French doors let sunlight pour in. Beyond it is the living room, with Parquet de Versailles floors, Venetian-plastered walls and a white marble fireplace. Six more Juliet balconies line the room, so the space feels open even on a quiet day. The formal dining room is another highlight. Its herringbone floors and goatskin-panelled walls give it a warm, almost old-world feel, according to the listing.Across the gallery sits an oak-panelled library. It has a bookshelf-lined alcove, access to a terrace and breathtaking views of the park. The lowest floor has a powder room and a galley kitchen that seems to run on for a long way. It ends in a breakfast room that opens through bronze and glass pocket doors. The top two levels contain the bedrooms and bathrooms. The primary suite takes up the entire top floor and opens onto its own large terrace.Before selling the apartment, the former owners spent two years renovating it, upgrading the finishes and mechanical systems. Buyers often look for updated wiring and plumbing in a building this old, so that work likely made the place easier to sell, even at a lower price.Johansson and Jost’s purchase was part of a broader trend of high-end Manhattan co-ops selling below their asking prices and sometimes their previous sale prices. For instance, a unit at 4 East 66th Street sold for $37 million after being listed for $55 million in 2022. Julia Koch sold her 18-room co-op at 740 Park Avenue for $45 million, about 25 per cent less than she had sought in 2022. Still, the drop is significant. The penthouse sold for less than half its original asking price of $27.5 million. Other sellers have taken losses, too. Grace Hightower, the former wife of Robert De Niro, also sold a co-op on Central Park West. She sold it for $18 million, below the $20.9 million she and De Niro had paid in 2006.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.
