articles.title: Suwayda remains in stasis as US signals differences with Israel on Syria
articles.summary: Governorate’s Druze majority in deadlock with Syrian government.
articles.body:
United States special envoy Tom Barrack recently spoke with a popular X personality about Syria and, in particular, Suwayda, which has been a hotbed of tensions between the government and Israel.

The southern governorate, which is majority Druze , is one of the last places in the country where the Syrian government does not have full control.

Barrack referred to “a particular Druze sheikh”, thought to be Hikmat al-Hijri , a leading political and religious figure in Suwayda. The National Guard, a Druze armed group linked to al-Hijri, has been accused of receiving support from Israel with separatist ambitions.

Barrack’s comment on al-Hijri is perceived by many as a firm message to Israel, which has attacked Syrian ministries and soldiers and tried to curry favour with Syria’s Druze community with the National Guard accused of acting as an Israeli proxy.

US President Donald Trump has built a strong relationship with his counterpart in Damascus, Ahmed al-Sharaa, and perceives any instability in Syria as dangerous for a country trying to rebuild after 13 years of war.

“[Barrack’s] message was totally clear,” Navvar Saban, a researcher in security and military affairs at the Arab Center for Contemporary Syrian Studies, told Al Jazeera. “Israel backing [al-Hijri] does not equal American backing. Washington has prioritised an agreement with Damascus while Israel retains its own security demands and relationship.”

Since the fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, the US has slowly rebuilt relations with Damascus and its new leader.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has received strong US support for his assaults in Lebanon, Palestine and Iran, has a view of the new Syrian government that is very different from Trump’s.

In the days immediately after the collapse of al-Assad’s government, Israel invaded Syria and seized land in Quneitra governorate and other strategically important areas of the country.

Israel has threatened President al-Sharaa’s government in Damascus, bombed the Ministry of Defence , and harassed and arrested Syrians in southern Syria . Israel has drawn an outcry from Syrian officials due to its repeated incursions into Syria.

Barrack, a Trump confidant who is the US ambassador to Turkiye and a special envoy to Syria and Iraq, has built a reputation for his direct approach to diplomacy, at times without regard to caution, as evidenced when he called some members of the media in Lebanon “animalistic” last year.

On Friday, Barrack spoke to Australian X personality Mario Nawfal and addressed the situation in southern Syria. He appeared to take the view that Washington favoured Damascus having control over Suwayda rather than a group aligned with al-Hijri and linked to Israel.

“[Barrack’s] remarks expose differences with Israel,” Nanar Hawach, a Syrian analyst told Al Jazeera. “Washington is building a partner in Damascus while Israel appears to prefer a Damascus that is too weak to assert itself in the south.”

Having grown tired of their worsening living conditions, residents in Suwayda, including many in its Druze majority, rose up against the al-Assad regime in 2023. They maintained their protests until the regime collapsed in December 2024.

Many in Suwayda celebrated this moment, which ended more than five decades of Baathist rule, although they were also hesitant to throw their support behind the new government.

That hesitancy turned to blatant opposition to al-Sharaa after fighting between Bedouin tribes and Druze in Suwayda turned into deadly sectarian killings in July 2025. Forces reportedly connected to the government joined the fighting on the side of the Bedouins. While there was violence and death on both sides, the casualties were overwhelmingly Druze.

Israel intervened in the fighting at one point, attacking what it said were Syrian government forces entering Suwayda. Since then, Israel has reportedly been trying to curry favour with locals there, including al-Hijri, who has been fervent in his opposition to Damascus’s new leadership.

“Israel appears intent on a lasting military presence in southern Syria, and it uses Suwayda as a lever against Damascus, offering enough support to keep the province reliant on Israeli protection and too little to secure its future,” Hawach said. “Along its line in Quneitra and Daraa [areas of southern Syria that Israel has invaded], Israel treats neighbouring communities differently, reviving wartime grievances between Syrians that any future Syria-Israel arrangement would struggle to undo.”

In Suwayda, analysts said, al-Hijri’s support is not universal but he benefits whenever the Druze community feels under attack.

“Sheikh al-Hijri’s authority rises with the community’s sense of threat and opens to debate as that threat recedes, so pressure from Damascus tends to strengthen the leadership it aims to weaken,” Hawach said. “Each side points to the other’s hard line to justify its own. That keeps Suwayda’s future framed in security terms and crowds out the many residents, clerics and local figures seeking a path between central rule and separation.”

Accountability needed for reconciliation

After the events of July 2025, the US began talks with the Syrian government hosted by Jordan to resolve the crisis. A trilateral agreement was signed in Amman in September 2025 that said Syria would invite an independent international commission to investigate what happened in Suwayda and perpetrators would be brought to justice.

While major fighting has not resumed between Damascus and Druze factions, the situation in Suwayda remains in a deadlock with many in the province having no trust in the government.

“Distrust has hardened, partly because Damascus has sought to bring Suwayda back by pressuring its leadership, and residents feel that pressure first, in their salaries, their children’s exams and the road to the capital,” Hawach said. “Trust tends to return through what the state delivers. Damascus stands a better chance of winning people back by serving residents directly and pursuing accountability for July 2025.”

Analysts said accountability is crucial if Damascus wants to bring Suwayda back into the Syrian fold.

“A durable settlement needs credible accountability for what happened in 2025,” Saban said. “The Druze need to be guaranteed protection of movement, education and security. Neither weakening Hijri, nor restoring government institutions alone will rebuild the trust.”

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says it struck Houthi missile facilities
articles.summary: Coalition says it destroyed ballistic missile launchers as well as tunnels and a depot used to store missiles.
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it carried out a military operation “aimed at neutralising sources of threat”, as the armed group claimed attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said on Monday its forces destroyed four ballistic missile launchers and five tunnels used by the Houthis to store missiles.

In a post on X, he also said coalition forces attacked a missile depot, adding that the operation “focused on cutting off Houthi militia supply lines between areas under their control”.

The operation also targeted Houthi “fortifications, gatherings of their members, and their military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen”.

The Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – have carried out a wave of strikes in recent weeks against Saudi airports and other infrastructure. This follows a major escalation in fighting in Yemen’s war, in which Saudi Arabia is supporting the internationally recognised government fighting the Houthis.

A Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport this month killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade.

The attacks led to the airport’s temporary closure, forcing the postponement of Saudi Arabia’s flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.

The airport reopened and flights resumed on Sunday with the Houthis warning travellers to avoid the facility, calling it a “military target.”

The Houthis later claimed they attacked the airport “with a ballistic missile, striking the target with precision”, according to a post by Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on social media on Monday.

Al-Maliki said on Monday that Saudi air defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh.”

Saree also said that the Houthis had struck oil pumping stations in Saudi Arabia with drones.

In a separate statement, Saree also claimed responsibility for more ballistic missile attacks on “enemy” forces and weapons depots in Yemen.

He said the attacks targeted positions in the Salah al-Din area of Aden governorate and the al-Wahat area of Lahij governorate.

Yemen’s war reignited in the summer when the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, which intervened in 2015 to lead a coalition aimed at restoring the internationally recognised government that was ousted from the capital Sanaa by the Houthis in 2014.

A 2022 truce that had halted most fighting collapsed last month, as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from government forces and also attacking Saudi energy facilities and airports.

Yemen’s government forces this month launched the “Operation Yemen Dawn” counteroffensive, aimed at recapturing territory held by the Houthis.

As operations resumed at Riyadh airport, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and discussed a key air defence system.

Mitsotakis “responded favourably to the kingdom’s request to keep the Patriot system in Saudi Arabia, given the current challenging circumstances”, his office said, referring to a battery of the US-made air defence system deployed by Greece to Saudi Arabia in 2021, which protects energy infrastructure in Yanbu, on the Red Sea coast.

On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition said air defences intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles.

The kingdom’s civil defence agency said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, also reporting damage to several buildings and vehicles.

Images released by the kingdom’s official press agency showed a building with part of its upper facade destroyed, exposing metal rods. Another image captured large windows shattered, with shards of glass strewn across the pavement and part of the road.

articles.title: Japan indicts U.S. Marine over Okinawa killing, media say
articles.summary: Japanese prosecutors have indicted a U.S. Marine on charges of robbery and murder of a Japanese woman in the country’s southernmost prefecture of Okinawa, Japanese media reported.
articles.body: TOKYO — Japanese prosecutors have indicted a U.S. Marine on charges of robbery and murder of a Japanese woman in the country’s southernmost prefecture of Okinawa, Japanese media reported. Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is suspected of killing Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel in Naha, the prefectural capital, earlier this month. Ballard has denied the allegations. Public broadcaster NHK reported prosecutors indicted Ballard on Sunday, adding that he allegedly strangled the victim with a telephone cord and stole a backpack containing a wallet, citing the Naha District Public Prosecutors’ Office. The Prosecutors’ Office could not be reached for comment outside business hours. The case set off protests in Okinawa and the nation’s capital, Tokyo, drew condemnation from Japanese political leaders and prompted a curfew and alcohol ban for U.S. soldiers stationed in Okinawa. It is the latest in a string of incidents stretching back years that have fueled unease over the large ⁠U.S. troop presence on the island chain near Taiwan and China. The III Marine Expeditionary Force said in a statement that it is aware Ballard has been indicted. “We recognize the seriousness of the charges and will continue to cooperate fully with Japanese authorities in their ongoing investigation as the legal process moves forward,” it said.

articles.title: What will we leave our children? The American Dream demands more than comfort
articles.summary: The American dream was built on generational sacrifice, but rising federal deficits and cultural retreat raise urgent questions about what we leave behind.
articles.body: As Americans prepare to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, much of the national conversation centers on which party will control Congress and what the next two years will mean for the country. Those are important questions, but a more consequential one reaches beyond the next election and our own lifetimes: What kind of America are we leaving to our children and grandchildren? For much of our history, the American Dream was rooted in the conviction that the next generation should inherit greater freedom and opportunity than the one before it. Men and women crossed oceans, endured hardship, established communities and sacrificed their own comfort because they believed their children could enjoy opportunities they might never experience. They understood that the measure of a generation was not simply what it accumulated, but what it preserved for those who followed. Consider the early settlers who crossed the Atlantic seeking religious freedom. They knew their journey would demand sacrifice, yet they believed the freedom to worship according to conscience was worth securing. Their convictions helped shape the American understanding that faith and conscience belong to the individual, not the government. ARKANSAS TAKES HOME TOP RANKING FOR RELIGIOUS FREEDOM AFTER GOV SANDERS EXPANDS KEY PROTECTIONS In his 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists, President Thomas Jefferson affirmed the constitutional protection of religious conscience against government interference. Religious liberty was never intended to remove faith from public life. It was intended to protect the right of every American to freely exercise their religious beliefs and worship without government subjugation. Later generations of immigrants came seeking economic opportunity. They worked difficult jobs, built businesses and raised families hoping their children might achieve more than they had. Their circumstances differed from those of the early settlers, but they shared a fundamental understanding of the American Dream: sacrificing something in the present to secure something greater for the future. SEN TIM SCOTT: MY FAMILY'S JOURNEY SHOWS AMERICA'S FOUNDING PROMISE IS ALIVE AND STRONG Somewhere along the way, we began losing that generational perspective. The American Dream increasingly became a question of what we could acquire and enjoy during our lifetimes rather than what we could build for those who followed. We became more concerned with protecting our immediate comfort than confronting the difficult decisions necessary to preserve our children's future. Our national finances illustrate that shift. The federal government continues operating with enormous annual deficits, adding to a national debt future generations will inherit. Reasonable people disagree over spending priorities, taxation and government's proper role. Yet every American should consider whether we are willing to make difficult decisions today or are content to pass their consequences to children who have no voice in making them. AMERICA’S DEBT CRISIS THREATENS OUR CHILDREN’S FUTURE. WE THE PEOPLE NEED TO FIX IT This is ultimately a question of stewardship that extends far beyond government spending. A free society cannot survive indefinitely on previous generations' sacrifices while refusing to make sacrifices of its own. Religious liberty, economic opportunity, strong families and healthy communities require more than appreciation for what we inherited. They require the conviction to preserve those blessings for people we may never meet. Christians should understand this responsibility. Scripture calls believers to care for others and pass the knowledge of God from one generation to the next. In John 13:34, Jesus commands His disciples to love one another as He has loved them. That love is demonstrated through what we are willing to give of ourselves for others. AMERICA’S NEXT 250 YEARS DEPEND ON PASSING FAITH AND FREEDOM TO OUR CHILDREN Yet I wonder whether we have become so accustomed to inherited freedoms that we have forgotten what preserving them requires. Previous generations endured persecution and extraordinary hardship to secure religious liberty. Today, Christians sometimes hesitate to express their convictions because doing so might cost them their reputation, influence or standing within their circles. We should consider what that reveals about our understanding of sacrifice. Pastors and Christian leaders know the pressure to avoid controversy. Biblical teaching can offend cultural sensibilities, challenge prevailing assumptions or invite criticism. Yet Hebrews 4:12 (KJV) reminds us that "the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword." SOUTHERN BAPTIST PRESIDENT CALLS ON PASTORS TO 'STEP UP' AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS Scripture was never intended to conform to the prevailing opinions of the culture, but to penetrate the hearts and consciences of those who hear it. The temptation is to soften the message, avoid difficult subjects and preserve comfort through silence. Yet Christian leadership has never been about making faith comfortable. It is about proclaiming biblical truth without compromise, equipping believers to live faithfully and preparing the next generation to understand the convictions entrusted to them. A free society cannot survive indefinitely on previous generations' sacrifices while refusing to make sacrifices of its own. The church cannot fulfill that responsibility by retreating from questions shaping American life. Christian communicators, whether standing behind a pulpit, speaking into a microphone or reaching audiences through digital media, must communicate truth with clarity and courage. articles.title: What to know about the Israeli elections as Netanyahu faces a battle for survival
articles.summary: After three years of navigating war, crisis and global outcry, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing one of the most significant electoral tests of his decades-long political career.
articles.body: TEL AVIV — After three years of navigating war, crisis and global outcry, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing one of the most significant electoral tests of his decades-long political career. As Israelis go to the polls on Tuesday, Netanyahu’s party is neck and neck with former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as his strongest rival in a campaign that has revolved around everything from Israel’s security and military conscription to bread-and-butter issues like the economy. Why is this election so important? This is the first nationwide election in Israel since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks, the deadliest day in the country’s history. The attacks, which saw 1,195 people killed and 251 taken into Gaza as hostages, triggered a major security crisis that led to three years of war on multiple fronts. There are few households in Israel that haven’t been affected in some way by the events that have played out since, leaving a sense of profound grief and insecurity that lingers across Israeli society. For most Israelis, the man who has defined the continuing legacy of October 7 is Netanyahu. Many of his opponents believe he has repeatedly evaded responsibility for the intelligence failures leading up to the attacks and what is widely seen as the security forces’ inadequate response. Bibi, as he’s commonly called, has led Israel for nearly 19 of the past 30 years, with security for many years a core part of his pitch to voters. The 77-year-old has survived political defeats before, only to come back stronger, but a groundswell of opposition could make this one of the most formidable challenges of his political career. The election is about more than just political survival for Netanyahu — it’s also about his personal freedom. Netanyahu is seeking re-election while also facing long-running criminal cases domestically on charges of fraud, breach of trust and bribery, allegations he has dismissed as a politically motivated witch-hunt. His grip on power affords him political privileges that have allowed him to drag out those cases, but that could change if he is voted out of power. Critics have derisively accused him of running to stay out of jail. What issues are at play? Netanyahu goes into the election as both the leading candidate and one of the biggest issues dividing voters. His actions before, during and after the Oct. 7 attacks have driven much of the debate. Netanyahu’s opponents — particularly his strongest rival, Eisenkot, 66 — have rallied around calls for an independent commission of inquiry to investigate the attacks, which Netanyahu has opposed. Various critics accuse Netanyahu of helping to keep Hamas in power in Gaza in the years before Oct. 7, of prioritizing the fight against Hamas over rescuing Israeli hostages in the wake of the attacks, and of alienating Israel from much of the world with his actions since. Last month, he threatened to sue Israeli newspaper Haaretz over a report that he had been warned about Oct. 7 ahead of time. “This is the first chance Israelis will have to vote in what is becoming a referendum on what Netanyahu has come to represent following Oct. 7,” said Dahlia Sheindlin, an Israeli American political analyst. “For his supporters, he is the strong prime minister who fought back and was able to expand the war to other fronts to defend Israel,” she said. “And to his detractors or critics, people supporting parties of the opposition, he’s the prime minister who led to the failures of the government to detect or prevent Oct. 7 and has refused to take accountability for it.” Netanyahu has staunchly defended his conduct and the war in Gaza, which has left about 74,500 people dead since Oct. 7, according to figures from the Palestinian Ministry of Health. He goes into the election facing an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity, and having vehemently rejected allegations of perpetrating a genocide from a United Nations commission. But while Israel’s conduct in Gaza has provoked strong international opposition, opinions within Israel remain highly supportive of Israel’s conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, the West Bank and Iran, with a broad surge in support for right-wing parties and a greater emphasis on Israeli security. Eisenkot, who served in Netanyahu’s war cabinet in the opening months of the war, has criticized strategic failures and supports a long-term ceasefire. He has vowed to remove Hamas from power within 18 months of taking office. Palestinian-led parties, which largely enjoy support from Palestinian-Israeli citizens who make up 20% of Israel’s population, go into the election as the loudest voices calling for restraint when dealing with Palestinians in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip. But Palestinian-Israeli voters in Israel will also cast votes with an eye on the rising scourge of organized crime in their communities that has caused a spike in violent deaths over the past few years. The vast majority of Palestinians in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip are not Israeli citizens and are not able to vote in the election. A key dividing line ahead of the election has been the compulsory conscription of the strictly orthodox Haredi Jews into the Israeli military. For generations, Israeli law has given leave to Haredi men to study scripture instead of military service, which is mandatory for other 18-year-olds. Many Israelis now want to end the exemption for a group that now accounts for nearly 15% of Israel’s population. While the tumultuous events of the last few years have dominated the headlines, many Israelis also will vote on bread-and-butter issues that Americans will find familiar: education, healthcare, crime, transportation and, above all, inflation. Israel’s still-thriving tech boom has left out huge portions of the population, particularly the young, who are being squeezed by soaring prices. What do the polls say? No one Israeli party can expect to earn a majority of the Israeli Knesset’s 120 seats — that’s never happened in Israeli history. Israel’s leadership will instead be decided by negotiations to build a governing coalition. For much of the past few months, the two top coalitions have been neck and neck. But the latest polling by Israel’s Wala news shows Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, pushing ahead, winning 23 seats compared to Netanyahu’s Likud winning 19. Behind the two front-runner parties is an alliance of two center-right former prime ministers who joined forces to form their own party called B’Yachad, or Together. The latest polls have Together winning 14 seats. The Democrats, the largest political party representing what remains of Israel’s leftist political current, is projected to win nine seats. Most of the remaining vote will go to a menagerie of smaller right-wing parties representing more niche religious and ethnic identities: Yisrael Beytenu, Otzma Yehudit, Shas, Religious Zionism and United Torah Judaism are each expected to win six to eight seats, according to Wala’s research. Palestinian-Israeli political parties like Ra’am and the Joint List are likely to get similar numbers, but will split the Palestinian-Israeli vote. How will the vote be conducted? The elections for the 26th Knesset will take place on Tuesday, with 7,331,981 Israeli citizens eligible to vote, and no fewer than 35 parties running candidates. Each voter will cast a ballot for one party in a nationwide poll. There are no separate geographic constituencies and voters do not cast ballots directly for named politicians — every ballot is cast only for a political party and is counted among the full national pool. Polls will open at 7 a.m. at more than 12,000 polling stations across the country, mostly schools, hospitals, prisons and other public buildings. The voting places will close at 10 p.m., at which point major news outlets will release their own exit polling data as polling officials begin counting the ballots. A complex vote apportioning system calculates the share of seats each party receives for its votes based on the total voter turnout. Parties that receive fewer than 3.25% of the vote will win no seats — a fate that at least two-thirds of the parties can probably expect. What happens next? The official results are required to be published within eight days of the vote, though the rough seat counts should be known well before then. But even those official results will be far from the last word on who will govern. Days and maybe weeks of horse-trading will follow, as the parties jockey to form a governing coalition with support from at least 61 of the 120 elected Knesset members. This step gives outsized influence to smaller parties, which can emerge as kingmakers able to press for concessions and ministerial posts in the government and can influence which coalitions get to form a government, or even attempt to string together enough support to try and govern by themselves. Approximately one week after the official results are published, President Isaac Herzog will task a member of the Knesset with forming a government. Herzog can pick whichever member’s proposed coalition he finds most promising — and is not required to choose the member with the largest party or the coalition. The member has a maximum of seven weeks to convene a ruling coalition before all lawmakers must vote on whether to accept it. That could allow for a minority government and give weaker coalitions a shot at leadership if they can rally the support of the full legislature. If that member cannot form a coalition able to win majority support in the Knesset, the president appoints another member to form a coalition. If that attempt fails as well, and the Knesset remains gridlocked, the president can dissolve the Knesset, with new elections taking place within 90 days. Such an impasse can drag on for years: Israelis went to the polls five times during the three years between 2019 and 2022. The outcome of those years of electoral discord: Netanyahu, the great survivor of Israeli politics, returned to office. Next week, he will be hoping his luck has not yet run out.

articles.title: Arizona officials sued after 25 US citizens were wrongly flagged as possible noncitizens and blocked from voting; following court-ordered mediation, their voting access was restored days before the November 3 midterms
articles.summary: With the November 3 midterm elections just days away, 25 US citizens in Arizona have regained their voting access after being wrongly identified as
articles.body: With the November 3 midterm elections just days away, 25 US citizens in Arizona have regained their voting access after being wrongly identified as possible noncitizens. Their registrations were restored following a legal dispute between Maricopa County Recorder Justin Heap and Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes. The two sides reached an agreement through court-ordered mediation on Friday, bringing the lawsuit to an end.These people had previously voted in US elections but later found their registrations restricted because officials questioned their citizenship. Investigations eventually confirmed that they were American citizens. However, that finding did not immediately resolve the problem, as Heap's office maintained that it needed documentary evidence before allowing them to vote again.According to Arizona Mirror, the disagreement reached Maricopa County Superior Court after Mayes sought to have the affected registrations restored before the election. The matter was settled when her office provided the citizenship information requested by Heap's office.Of the 25 people covered by the lawsuit, 24 had their active voter status restored following mediation. The remaining person had already regained voting access after independently submitting proof of citizenship. The recorder's office also issued early ballots to 18 affected voters who were enrolled in the county's Active Early Voting List.Voters identified as noncitizensThe dispute is related to a review of Arizona's voter registrations. Heap's office had used a federal database called the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) to identify people who might not be US citizens.The database, which had been modified under the Trump administration to help identify possible noncitizens registered to vote, has also incorrectly flagged American citizens.Using this system, Heap's office identified 207 registered voters as possible noncitizens. Their information was then forwarded to the Maricopa County Attorney's Office for further examination.Among those flagged, 60 had participated in earlier elections. Heap changed their registration status, leaving them unable to vote unless they produced the required documents establishing their citizenship.However, when the Maricopa County Attorney's Office examined those 60 cases, it found that 52 people were US citizens. Only eight were identified as noncitizens. The investigation also found that no more than three of those eight had voted in the same election.The Arizona Attorney General's Office reached similar conclusions. But even after the citizenship of the affected voters had been verified, 25 people remained without restored voting access.Matter ended up in courtThe two offices disagreed over what was required to reinstate the voters. According to KJZZ 91.5 FM, Heap's lawyer told the court that although investigators had established the voters' citizenship, they had not shared the documents supporting those findings with the recorder's office. Heap maintained that the registrations could be restored once the necessary evidence was received.Meanwhile, Mayes disputed the handling of the case. Her office argued that Heap should not have restricted the registrations before confirming that the people concerned were not American citizens.Under the state law cited by the Attorney General's Office, a recorder must confirm that someone is not a US citizen before cancelling their voter registration. Mayes' office argued that suspicion alone did not meet that requirement.With the election approaching and the disagreement unresolved, Mayes filed a lawsuit seeking to restore voting access to the 25 citizens.Two sides reach an agreementAt a court hearing on Friday, the Attorney General's Office indicated that it could provide the driver's licence information used to verify the voters' citizenship.Later that day, both sides met with Judge Christopher Whitten, who had been appointed to mediate the dispute. Once the documentation was provided, Heap's office reinstated the remaining affected voters.Heap defended his decision to wait for the records saying, “We needed legally sufficient documentation of citizenship, we received it, and we immediately restored the voters. Our office fulfilled its duty to protect eligible voters while upholding Arizona law."Mayes, however, continued to question why court intervention had been necessary. “It should not have taken litigation to make Justin Heap follow the law; that is his duty and the duty of all election officials,” she said. Maricopa County Supervisor Tom Galvin also criticised Heap for his handling of the registrations.Following the agreement, Mayes agreed to dismiss the lawsuit, while the recorder's office confirmed that the affected citizens had regained active voter status.The settlement also allowed early ballots to be issued to 18 voters on the Active Early Voting List. October 23 was the deadline for requesting an early ballot, and county officials advised voters to return mailed ballots by October 27.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Serbia after Vucic: Who will be PM and when will a government be formed?
articles.summary: Uncertainty remains over key positions after student-led movement deals a blow to longtime leader’s political dominance.
articles.body:
A student-led opposition movement has emerged victorious in Serbia’s snap parliamentary election, ending former President Aleksandar Vucic’s long grip on power.

The Student List’s win on Sunday followed nearly two years of youth-led protests triggered by the death of 16 people in a railway station canopy collapse in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.

Demonstrations demanding accountability quickly evolved into a wider political campaign against alleged corruption and capture of democratic institutions. In its electoral programme presented in September, the Student List said fighting corruption and organised crime were among its main priorities. It also pledged to raise living standards, boost employment, improve education, ensure media freedom and the independence of Serbia’s institutions.

After declaring victory on Sunday, the movement also said it would work to improve relations with neighbouring countries following a period of tension during Vucic’s more than decade-long rule.

The Republic Election Commission (RIK) announced on Monday that the Student List had won 52.54 percent of the vote, based on 8,077 processed polling stations out of 8,392.

The figures also showed the United Serbia list, led by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party, had secured 39.29 percent of ballots cast.

Voter turnout stood at 68.78 percent, a record high in more than 30 years, according to RIK data on Sunday.

While the final election result is not yet known, the figures mean that the Student List will be able to form a majority in Serbia’s 250-seat parliament on its own.

The bloc is projected to win 140 seats, well ahead of the 126 mandates required for a majority, while United Serbia is expected to have 103.

The remaining seats are set to go to the Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians (three); the Albanian political bloc (two); and the Rasim Ljajc-Ljudski and SDA Sandzak lists, with one each.

Unlike United Serbia, which named Vucic as its candidate for prime minister before the election, the Student List made no such announcement during the campaign.

Since its formal creation, the list has avoided highlighting single candidates, eager to emphasise the collective nature of the movement that brought together academics, doctors and workers.

During the campaign, the movement was led by Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Novi Sad. The cardiologist is now seen as the most likely candidate to become the next prime minister, but it remains unclear who will take over key ministries, including those of internal affairs, finance and justice.

This depends on when the final election results will be announced and when parliament convenes.

The new National Assembly must be established within 30 days of the final results being announced.

A government must be formed within 90 days after that – but the Student List’s clear majority removes the need for lengthy coalition talks.

Vucic has dominated Serbia’s politics – first as prime minister and then as president – since 2014.

Following his call for the snap parliamentary vote last month and his resignation as president, the post has been held temporarily by Ana Brnabic, the president of the National Assembly.

Brnabic is obliged to call for an extraordinary presidential election which must be held no later than three months after the end of Vucic’s mandate.

Vucic resigned on September 27 , so the deadline to hold a vote is December 27 .

The president of Serbia is elected directly by the citizens, not by the representatives in the assembly, but the post is largely ceremonial.

articles.title: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US
articles.summary: This is how his signature policy has played out after returning to power promising a closed border and mass deportations.
articles.body:
Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.

When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico for of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.

Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.

But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.

Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.

He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.

But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.

His signature policy has played out in five key ways.

Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.

His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.

When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.

By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.

On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.

To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.

That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north.

"President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October.

"The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."

A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.

Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.

According to government figures , about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.

Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.

Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.

Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate.

"Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.

There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.

Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it.

"I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."

Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning

3. Detentions and deportations rocketing

Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.

During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.

Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project , a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.

But the same data shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.

Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.

But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead.

A New York Times and Siena poll released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength.

A separate poll, from Politico and Public First in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive.

After returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests.

In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied.

The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation".

Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African.

By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela.

Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to.

One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.

Haitian migrants changed this US town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again

5. A squeeze on visas - and a $1m golden ticket

Other legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes.

Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel.

Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down.

And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers , mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X that registrations for 2027 were down 40%.

"The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added.

While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive.

One study, from the Wharton School of Business , found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth.

Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million.

The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee.

At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.

articles.title: Shoppers replace buses as London pedestrianizes part of Britain’s ​busiest shopping street
articles.summary: Part of London’s Oxford Street went permanently traffic-free in an effort to revitalize the area and create a new public space to boost economic growth.
articles.body: Part of London’s Oxford Street, Britain’s ​busiest shopping thoroughfare, went permanently traffic-free on Monday in an effort to revitalize the area and create a new public space to boost economic growth. An almost milelong section is now closed to buses, cars, taxis, cycles, scooters and pedicabs, the office of London Mayor Sadiq Khan said. The move has been more than two decades in the making. ⁠It and a wider regeneration project aim ​to ⁠put Oxford Street back among top global shopping destinations including New York’s Times Square, Paris’ Champs-Élysées and Barcelona’s La Rambla. “After ⁠so many false dawns, and now working with a government who ​share ⁠the scale of my ambition, ‌I’m proud that we’re finally unlocking a new era for the street,” Khan said. “Revitalizing Oxford Street will boost jobs and economic growth ‌in the capital.” Oxford Street, connected to ‌Bond Street and Regent Street and home to John Lewis, Marks & Spencer, Tiffany & Co and many others, has struggled since the Covid pandemic, with the arrival of U.S. ⁠candy stores putting off many shoppers. The pedestrianization is the first stage of a transformation, although minimal construction will take place during the run-up to Christmas, a busy shopping period. Plans for 2027 include more than 50 new trees, 100 new seats, two public squares, rest areas and better signage and lighting. Oxford Street attracts around half a million ‌visitors every day, according to the mayor’s office, but many ​flagship stores including House of Fraser and Topshop have shut ‌in recent years, and Khan ⁠said the area had been neglected. “This marks an exciting ⁠new chapter for Oxford Street, creating a greener, more vibrant place that will attract visitors ‌and investment, support businesses ​and jobs, and drive growth in ‌the heart of our capital,” ​British housing, Communities and Local Government minister Angela Rayner said.

articles.title: Storms can prove 'devastating' for some marine species
articles.summary: Storms bring challenges to marine life as the sea gets mixed up by winds, a Guernsey scientist says.
articles.body:
Guernsey's rocky coast could have helped some marine life by providing holes to hide out the worst of Storm Austen, where gusts reached 76mph (122km/h), a marine scientist has said.

Oceanongrapher Liz Sweet told BBC Guernsey the conditions "can be dangerous, particularly with the big storms" and said species such as crabs would have found the mixing up of the sea and sediment challenging.

Octopuses may have fared better seeking shelter in holes and Sweet, who is also known as the Guernsey Scientist, explained that sharks and dolphins would have swum out to calmer water.

She added storms could be "really devastating" for seal pups.

Sweet added: "Sea birds seem to love storms.

"Depending on the storm, they often fly towards it and often eat much better."

She said the fishing in the days following a storm was "generally much better".

It comes as the British Divers Marine Life Rescue charity in the Channel Islands appealed to islanders to keep an eye out for seal pups which may have got buffeted by the weather and become separated from their mothers.

A pup died on Jersey before it could be sent to Guernsey's GSPCA to be cared for there.

articles.title: Israeli forces kill at least five people in Gaza, including 7-year-old girl
articles.summary: The death toll in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza climbs to 74,555, including 1,559 killed since ‘ceasefire’ last year.
articles.body:
At least five people have been killed in Gaza and more than a dozen have been wounded in Israeli ground and air attacks.

Four Palestinians, including a young girl, were killed on Monday in an Israeli air attack on a camp for displaced people in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, according to medical sources and first responders.

Another person was killed and others were wounded on Monday in an Israeli drone attack on the Remal neighbourhood, west of Gaza City, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

Al-Shifa Hospital said the man was killed when the drone struck a group of displaced people in a tent.

Palestinian Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal said earlier on Monday that a total of 11 people had been killed and 50 wounded by Israeli fire and air strikes in Gaza over the past 24 hours.

“We transported three martyrs, including a child, following an Israeli air strike targeting a camp for displaced people in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis,” Basal told the AFP news agency.

Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis confirmed the three deaths, which have since risen to at least four, a source at the Gaza emergency services told Al Jazeera.

“Their bodies were torn apart by direct hits from shrapnel from the Israeli missile,” the hospital said, adding that several wounded people, including a child and a woman, had also come in for treatment.

The hospital identified three of the deceased as Hossam al-Zamli, 21, Tamer Abu Sneima, 24, and Jouri al-Soufi, who was only seven years old, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Education.

Israeli forces also set fire to a camp for displaced people at the Shujayea junction on Sunday night, forcibly displacing more than 200 families, or over 800 people, most of them women, children, elderly people and patients.

Gaza’s Ministry of Public Works and Housing said Israeli quadcopter drones set the camp ablaze at about 8pm, with fires consuming tents and belongings for several hours, continuing past midnight.

The ministry condemned the incident and called for urgent international aid to provide the displaced families with shelter and essential supplies.

As of Monday, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 74,555 people and injured 175,727. Medical sources said the number of people killed since the United States-brokered “ceasefire” on October 11 last year has risen to 1,559, and the number of injured to 5,608, while a large number of victims remain trapped under the rubble and on the streets, with ambulance and rescue crews unable to reach them.

articles.title: Bleach: Popular anime series officially ends as fans say goodbye
articles.summary: Twenty-two years after it first aired, one of the biggest animes of all time is coming to an end.
articles.body:
It's a finale fans have waited more than a decade to see.

The epic conclusion to Bleach, the popular animated series based on the hit manga, or Japanese comic, is due to land on streaming later.

And anticipation for the final episode of the climactic Thousand-Year Blood War storyline is especially high.

The original comic book's "rushed" ending is widely considered disappointing but original creator Tite Kubo has overseen some major changes to the new adaptation.

So, as some mourn the "end of an era", they're also nervously waiting to see if he can stick the landing second time around.

BBC Newsbeat's been speaking to fans as they say an "emotional" goodbye to Kubo's creation.

Bleach is regarded as one of the "big three" manga in Japan alongside One Piece and Naruto, and animated adaptations of each are credited with helping to fuel the global popularity of anime.

It follows the story of Ichigo Kurosaki, a teenager with distinctive orange hair who has the unusual ability to see ghosts.

He navigates school and family life at the same time as defending humanity from evil spirits.

"It is honestly my favourite series of all time, it has got me through a lot across my life," says Ruby.

The 27-year-old started reading Bleach aged nine and became friends with fellow fan Nicholas Thong, 30, through their shared passion.

"I've made so many friends through Bleach, it's been such a wonderful part of my life both in terms of what it teaches me and the kind of people I meet through it," says Ruby.

For Nicholas, watching Bleach as teenager helped him get through school - and he even has a tattoo dedicated to the story.

"It helped me make friends in school, talking to a few people who also knew Bleach and about our favourite characters," he says.

The pair tell Newsbeat they will be "crying together" as they watch the finale later.

"A lot of us are feeling quite emotional about it," says Ruby.

The original Bleach anime ran from 2004 to 2012 across 16 seasons but never caught up to the manga source material - with fans left unsure if it would ever come back.

But the first part of Bleach's animated final chapter eventually premiered 10 years later in 2022.

The arc, Thousand-Year Blood War, has been split into four separate chapters, and the final run began this July.

Bleach's original comic book ending was divisive and broadly unpopular with fans and was said to have been rushed due to creator Kubo experiencing health issues during its production.

One of the reasons they've been so excited to see the new, animated finale is due to the fact Kubo and animation house Pierrot Films have made changes to the original storyline.

And many are hoping the "final battle" will "fix" the unpopular ending from 2016.

Regardless of the final verdict, fans say Bleach will have a lasting legacy.

Itanna Alakija describes himself as the "biggest Bleach fan there is" and says one of his favourite things is how it represents black characters.

"The way that Tite Kubo integrates all these cultures and represents them in a Japanese art form is really interesting and amazing," the 28-year-old says.

Alakija was already a Naruto fan when he discovered Bleach as a teenager.

"I remember stumbling upon Bleach and thought: 'This looks cool'," he says.

And he praises the show for treating black characters as "normal people".

"It's one of the few anime that has represented black characters in a non-stereotypical way."

Bleach is available to stream via Disney+ globally and on Hulu in the US.

articles.title: Tallahassee police arrest 15-year-old suspect after shooting near Florida A&M football stadium
articles.summary: A 15-year-old male arrested Sunday night faces up to 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder after the Saturday night shooting near Bragg Memorial Stadium.
articles.body: The Tallahassee Police Department on Sunday night arrested a 15-year-old suspect in connection with a Florida A&M shooting Saturday near the university's Bragg Memorial Stadium. "What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families," Chief of Police Lawrence Revell said in a Monday morning statement. "While this arrest marks a significant step forward, our work is far from over. We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy." The teen is facing 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent, police said. 5 VICTIMS RELEASED FROM HOSPITAL AFTER FLORIDA A&M UNIVERSITY SHOOTING, 1 REMAINS CRITICAL The gunfire erupted around 8 p.m. ET on Saturday near Perry and Manatee streets, leaving 12 people injured. Eleven individuals suffered gunshot wounds, while one person sustained an ankle injury while attempting to flee the gunfire. It is not yet clear how many shooters fired shots or the extent of the teen's involvement in the shooting. At least five victims have been released from the hospital, while six others remained hospitalized Sunday night, including one in critical condition, Revell said in a video update posted to X. SHOOTING NEAR BALTIMORE YOUTH FOOTBALL EVENT LEAVES 12-YEAR-OLD GIRL DEAD, 3 ADULTS WOUNDED A fight broke out before the shooting and detectives believe the shooting resulted from a dispute between individuals who knew each other. None of the 12 victims appear to have been the intended targets, according to police. Officers responding to the scene Saturday evening provided immediate medical aid to victims before the perimeter was fully secured. Sworn and civilian personnel — including detectives, crime analysts and victim advocates — have worked around the clock since the incident to process the scene and identify those involved. Police officials credited community cooperation for accelerating the case, citing a substantial influx of tips and public digital evidence submitted in the hours following the gunfire. VIRGINIA STATE UNIVERSITY SHOOTING SUSPECT FOUND HIDING IN DORM CLOSET ARRESTED The investigation remains active and ongoing, noting that additional arrests are possible as detectives continue to review physical evidence, trace leads and establish the full sequence of events. "We will determine what happened, identify those responsible, and get answers for all of the victims, their families and everyone impacted by this tragedy," Revell wrote in a statement Sunday. "We know there are people who saw something, heard something or may have video that could help us piece together exactly what happened." TPD urges anyone with information to call the department’s dedicated tip line at 850-891-4610 or upload photos and video evidence via the agency's online portal. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We need our community's help," Revell added. "No detail is too small, and no piece of information should go unreported. If you know something, please share it with our detectives. Your information could be the key to holding those responsible accountable."

articles.title: Nikole Hannah-Jones laments 'pretty brutal' response to viral essay on sending daughter to public school
articles.summary: Nikole Hannah-Jones called the backlash to her New York Times Magazine essay on her decision to send her daughter to Black public schools "pretty brutal."
articles.body: New York Times journalist and 1619 Project founder Nikole Hannah-Jones reflected Wednesday on what she called the "pretty brutal" responses she received for her viral New York Times Magazine essay on sending her daughter to predominantly Black public schools. A decade after defending her choice, Hannah-Jones admitted in an essay last month that she regretted aspects of her decision to send her now-16-year-old daughter to these schools in an effort to combat school segregation, after her child informed Hannah-Jones that she did not receive the education she wanted. "Now I felt overcome with regret. Najya deserved better," Hannah-Jones wrote in her September essay. "They all did. But she was mine. This girl, my only child, looked to me to protect her, to give her what she needed to thrive. And I had not chosen her." KAROL MARKOWICZ: 1619 PROJECT FOUNDER NIKOLE HANNAH-JONES LEARNED THE HARD TRUTH ABOUT SCHOOLS Hannah-Jones' admission sparked intense backlash from critics who accused her of sacrificing her daughter's education for her progressive values. The pushback was strong enough for Hannah-Jones to question if she should have written the essay. "I know it would sound crazy if I say none of the critique was valid, but I’m like, what is the critique?" Hannah-Jones told The New York Times during an interview on Wednesday. "There was some online discourse that was pretty brutal. And, you know, I have experienced some brutal discourse through the years, but usually not about, like, me as a parent," Hannah-Jones said. "That was hard. And for a minute I’m like, ‘Man, should I have written this?’ And I’ve actually never, ever, as a journalist, questioned, 'Should I have written something?' And there was a moment where I was just like, ‘I did not have to subject myself to this. Should I have done this?’" However, Hannah-Jones concluded that she ultimately did not regret her actions despite the impact the essay had. NIKOLE HANNAH-JONES' FRIEND SENDS BLACK SON TO PRIVATE SCHOOL AFTER NYT WRITER HAS EDUCATION REGRETS "You know, in the end, I’m fine. I will be fine. My feelings got a little hurt because I’m a human being. But, in the end, like, people are talking about these kids who don’t have a platform, who don’t have a choice. The mayor of New York has been forced to respond. He’s now promised to release a plan to address it. That doesn’t happen without me writing a piece like this," Hannah-Jones said. She added, "And so, yeah, I have to remind myself that, like, my little bruised feelings in the end are meaningless. It is the power of what we can do with our platform, and what I would argue is our responsibility to do." Fox News Digital reached out to Hannah-Jones for comment, but did not immediately hear back. DENVER MOTHER FIGHTS FOR HER DAUGHTER'S EDUCATION AS ADVOCATES MAKE NATIONWIDE SCHOOL CHOICE PUSH Corey DeAngelis, a research fellow at The Heritage Foundation and longtime school choice advocate, accused the journalist of minimizing education concerns. "Calling the backlash 'brutal discourse' misses the point. People reacted because she publicly used her child as a prop for a political experiment, and the results were horrible," DeAngelis told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He added, "School choice exists so parents can leave schools that don't work. You don't fix these schools by trapping more kids inside them and hoping your presence changes the system. Hannah-Jones tried that. It didn't work. Her daughter knows it. Parents across the country already knew it. Give families the money and the freedom to leave."

articles.title: Russia’s 70-year-old Bear: The Tu-95 bomber that still patrols near America’s doorstep
articles.summary: Russia has sent its Cold War-era Tu-95MS strategic bombers, known by the Nato reporting name 'Bear', on a planned patrol near Alaska, highlighting the
articles.body: Russia has sent its Cold War-era Tu-95MS strategic bombers, known by the Nato reporting name 'Bear', on a planned patrol near Alaska, highlighting the continued role of the decades-old aircraft in Moscow’s long-range military operations.According to Reuters, Russian news agency RIA cited the defence ministry as saying on Monday that the bombers had carried out a planned patrol over the Bering and Chukchi seas in Russia’s Far East.The Bering and Chukchi seas lie close to Alaska, placing the patrol in a strategically important region between Russia and the United States. The area connects the North Pacific with the Arctic and remains significant for military activity by both countries.For Russia, such patrols demonstrate its ability to operate long-range strategic bombers near North America. They also allow crews to conduct extended flights over important maritime regions.But why is Russia still flying a bomber design that dates back more than seven decades, and what makes the Tu-95MS relevant to modern warfare?Why Russia still relies on its 70-year-old bomberFirst flown on November 12, 1952, the Tupolev Tu-95 was developed by the Soviet Union during the Cold War as a long-range strategic bomber capable of carrying nuclear weapons.Its later Tu-95MS variant, which first flew in 1979, was designed to carry long-range cruise missiles, transforming the aircraft into a standoff weapons platform. More than 500 aircraft of the wider Tu-95 family were produced, according to United Aircraft Corporation (UAC).The Tu-95 family served extensively with Soviet long-range aviation during the Cold War, carrying out strategic training missions, reconnaissance flights and patrols over the Arctic, Atlantic and Pacific.After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Russia retained the aircraft as part of its strategic aviation fleet. Russian Tu-95MS bombers later saw combat use in Syria in November 2015, launching cruise missiles against targets during Moscow's military campaign, and have been used to launch long-range cruise missiles against targets in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.The Tu-95MS is powered by four Kuznetsov NK-12MP turboprop engines, each producing approximately 15,000 horsepower and driving contra-rotating propellers.According to Rostec, the aircraft can reach a maximum speed of around 890 km/h, making it the fastest production turboprop-powered aircraft. Its reported range varies from 6,500 to 10,500 km depending on the weapons load and mission profile, giving it the endurance required for long-distance patrols over the Arctic and Pacific.The Tu-95MS has a maximum weapons payload of approximately 15,000 kg (15 tonnes). Depending on the variant, weapons can be carried internally in the fuselage weapons bay or externally on underwing pylons.Why the Tu-95MS remains relevant in modern warfareDespite being based on a design first flown in 1952, the Tu-95MS remains relevant because Russia uses it primarily as a long-range cruise-missile launch platform rather than a bomber that must fly directly over its targets.The aircraft can launch weapons such as the Kh-101 from a distance, allowing it to strike targets without entering the most heavily defended airspace.The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) identifies the Tu-95MS as Russia's primary launch platform for the Kh-101 cruise missile in the war against Ukraine.For Russia, keeping the Tu-95MS in service offers a way to sustain long-range strike capacity without depending entirely on newer and more expensive strategic bombers.Its continued patrols near Alaska also serve a signalling role, demonstrating that Russia can still deploy strategic aircraft across vast distances. Its relevance today comes less from the age of its airframe than from the long-range weapons it can carry and launch.

articles.title: A California federal judge ordered a pause in Trump administration investigations of suspected noncitizen voter registration across nine states, citing unreliable data, but put her own order on hold to allow an appeal
articles.summary: A federal judge in California has ordered a temporary stop to federal investigations into suspected noncitizen voter registration across nine states.
articles.body: A federal judge in California has ordered a temporary stop to federal investigations into suspected noncitizen voter registration across nine states. She ruled that officials relied on unreliable data and risked frightening eligible voters. US District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, who is based in Oakland, issued an order blocking the federal investigations until polls close on Election Day, 3 November. However, she put her own ruling on hold until Friday, 23 October, to give federal lawyers time to file an emergency appeal. The decision affects federal investigations in nine states: California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.Flawed data driving investigationsThe court's action followed growing concerns about how the federal investigation was being carried out. The programme, officially called the "Unlawful Voter Initiative," became public after Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and Democratic Senator Alex Padilla of California released a whistleblower report describing the scale of the operation. In her ruling, Judge Martínez-Olguín raised serious concerns about how federal agents chose people for investigation. According to reports by the Associated Press, The Washington Post and The Guardian, federal agents used databases with many errors and missing information to identify people suspected of being noncitizens who were registered to vote. The court noted that investigators had as little as 12 minutes per person to check whether someone was legally allowed to vote before starting field inquiries. Judge Martínez-Olguín found that such quick checks created a serious risk of wrongly targeting eligible U.S. citizens. These could include people who had recently become citizens or whose state records had not yet been updated in federal systems.Protecting voter participationA group of civic organisations and labor unions brought the case against the federal government. The groups included the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United, the Voto Latino Foundation, the City and County of San Francisco, and Santa Clara County. The plaintiffs argued that aggressive field interviews and checks based on unverified information created fear among voters. They said these actions could discourage eligible citizens and community volunteers from taking part in regular voter registration activities. According to Democracy Docket and The Guardian, Judge Martínez-Olguín agreed with the civic groups. She found that the Department of Homeland Security's investigation methods amounted to ongoing intimidation and threatened serious, lasting harm to eligible voters ahead of the upcoming elections. The judge made clear that her order does not allow noncitizens to register or vote in federal elections. Both remain illegal under federal law. Instead, the order limits how the government carries out its investigations to protect eligible voters from being harassed because of incorrect records.Federal defence and administrative contextThe federal government defended its actions in court. Officials argued that these investigations were needed to protect election integrity and enforce federal immigration laws. Representatives of the Department of Homeland Security said that investigating possible unlawful voter registration was within the executive branch's legal powers. Administration officials have claimed that noncitizen voting poses a widespread threat to elections. However, research and earlier federal reviews show that noncitizen voting is extremely rare. Such voting has never occurred on a scale large enough to change an election result. To give government lawyers time to ask the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for an emergency stay, Judge Martínez-Olguín temporarily paused the enforcement of her order through Friday, 23 October.Broader legal implicationsThe federal court's order is one of the most important recent limits on government programmes designed to check voter eligibility. By requiring officials to verify their data carefully, the court established that federal authorities cannot ignore established state verification systems or carry out broad door-to-door investigations based on unconfirmed lists. Voting rights advocates welcomed the ruling. They stressed that federal checks must respect the constitutional rights of eligible voters. Legal experts expect the case to move quickly through the appeals courts as early voting deadlines approach in several affected states. articles.title: 'Modi kahi nahi jaayega': BJP's message to 'anti-Indian' forces ahead of INDIA bloc's rally on Nov 1
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Monday posted a striking message amid the political sparring ahead of the INDIA bloc’s November 1 rally in Delhi.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Monday posted a striking message amid the political sparring ahead of the INDIA bloc’s November 1 rally in Delhi. It declared on its official X account, “Sorry to break it to you, all anti-Indian forces, BUT Modi kahi nahi jayega (Modi won't go anywhere)”.The post aimed to take a swipe at the opposition amid a row over Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's remark, "Modi ka baap bhi jayega."Meanwhile, pressure on the Congress to postpone its rally to after Diwali has been growing as traders have raised concerns that closures will disrupt businesses.BJP's jibe comes ahead of Congress' "mega rally" at Ramlila Maidan, which the opposition plans to use to intensify its campaign against alleged irregularities in the SIR of electoral rolls and demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Delhi traders demand postponement of INDIA bloc rallyThe rally has also triggered protests from Delhi's traders, who fear that security arrangements, road closures and traffic diversions could disrupt business during the crucial festive season. Traders demonstrated at Kashmere Gate on Monday, urging the Congress to reschedule the event and allow markets to operate without disruption.During the protest, traders raised the slogan, "20,000 vaipariyo ki ik hi pukar, Diwali ke baad kijiye rally ka vichar (20,000 traders have one appeal: hold the rally after Diwali)".The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) chairman, Brijesh Goyal, said the traders would write to leaders of all parties in the INDIA bloc, besides Congress president Kharge and Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi, asking them to defer the rally."We will write to leaders of all the parties in the INDIA bloc, urging them to hear our sentiments and postpone the rally," Goyal said.He expressed concern over the Congress's claim that around 10 lakh people could attend the rally, arguing that the gathering could severely affect wholesale markets around Ramlila Maidan."Business will be heavily impacted because, as reports suggest, 10 lakh people might gather at Ramlila Maidan, whereas its actual capacity is around 50,000," Goyal said.He cited a gathering at Jantar Mantar on October 10, claiming that the presence of around 2,000 to 4,000 people had led to metro station closures, barricading and restrictions. More than 20 major markets were forced to shut down, he alleged.According to Goyal, a rally of the anticipated scale could affect more than 20 wholesale hubs within a 5-km radius of Ramlila Maidan. These include Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazar, Khari Baoli, Naya Bazar, Chawri Bazar, Daryaganj and Kashmere Gate.He said road closures could prevent three to four lakh buyers from outside Delhi, who visit the capital daily, from reaching the markets. Local customers could also stay away because of traffic restrictions.Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, responded to the traders' concerns in a post on X on Monday, saying the protests would "stop in 30 seconds" if they asked Modi to sack chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the "vote chori" issue.Paramjeet Singh Pamma, president of the Sadar Bazar Bari Market Trade Association, also appealed to the Congress leadership to postpone the rally. He said the festive season was crucial for traders to recover their business across the year.Pamma warned that restrictions around major wholesale markets, including Sadar Bazar, Chandni Chowk, Khari Baoli, Fatehpuri and Azad Market, could cause losses worth crores of rupees, as traders and buyers from Delhi and other states flock to these areas during the festive season.The traders have urged the Congress to hold the rally after Diwali to avoid disrupting business during one of the busiest periods of the year.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
